The Minister of Marine will pardon me if I call his attention to the accident that happened to the steamer Saturnia in the harbour of Quebec. -owing to the fact that we are drawing near to the end of a century of peace between Canada and the United States. The columns of the press, and the atmosphere generally, is so full of platitudes about peace that the poor (fellow who wishes to keep up the militia is regarded as almost a blood-thirsty mortal who is not entitled to any consideration. However, I have more or less confidence! when I review the first few years of this great century of peace. I find, despite the cry of peace, of which we hear so much to-day, that the first thirteen years of this century have witnessed appalling wars: the South African waT; the Phillipine war; the Cuban war; the Russo-Japanese war; the Turko-Italian war; the Moroccan-French war: the Somaliland war; the Balkan-BulgaTian-Servian-Greek war; the Mexican war; the German South West African war; and the wars in China, Tibet and of the United States in Cuba, and now the war of the United States in Mexico.
Do not forget the Ulster war.

It is not on yet. My
hon. friend from Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) will doubtless watch with interest, and from a long range, the Ulster war when it comes on. I might point out to the hon. member that the Ulster men are of the same class as those who followed Stonewall Jackson-
Down in Virginia?

Yes, down in Virginia.
And if hon. gentlemen want to form an

opinion as to how the Ulster men will fight, let them read the record of Stonewall Jackson's division in the American Civil war. A strange incident recently occurred in connection with the Mexican war. In this country we have been more or less interested in the peace agitation. It was only a few years ago that we had some distinguished Americans, accompanied by distinguished Canadians, occupying the pulpits and platforms of the country preaching peace on the eve	of an	election, the objectevidently being to further the question	of free	trade between Canada
and the United States. This peace organization of the United States is the only institution I know of that has endorsed the incipient war of the United States on Mexico. Before the very first shot was fired this organization forgot its principles, and, in place of imploring the Government to hold its hand and to submit the matter to arbitration, they immediately wired President Wilson as follows:
Our league is an ardent peace organization, but not of the ' peace at any price ' kind.
Of course, the peace at any price kind would involve some great national principle, having for its object the uplifting of humanity; and I presume the question as to who fired the first salute would constitute a casus belli worthy of the endorsation of this great peace organization.
Turning to our own border, I do not think there is any great evidence of the human mind being in a position to guarantee perpetual peace in Canada. In this House we occasionally have illustrations that the human mind is not so disciplined, even amongst gentlemen who are supposed to be the highest in the land, as to guarantee internal peace. I have not the slightest doubt that some hon. gentlemen opposite will have the hardihood to even criticise my Estimates when they come up. Let us look for a moment at our courts of law and the convictions made in the Dominion of Canada. In 1911-12 alone, 113,260 persons in the Dominion of Canada were convicted in the courts of this country. The cost of the administration of justice in Canada the year before last-last year's figures have not yet been published -was a little in advance of the cost of the whole militia. The cost of administering justice in Canada in 1911-12 was $9,420,000, which is slightly in excess of the cost of the militia of the whole country. The customs and excise returns show that the [Mr. Sam. Hughes. I
customs duties on liquors in 1912-13 amounted to $9,270,600, and the excise duties, $11,488,104, or a total of $20,758,704. On tobaccos, customs duties amounted to $1,551,109, and the excise duties to $9,794,450, or a total of $11,345,559; making a grand total for liquors and tobaccos of $32,104,263. I do not necessarily imply that these breed criminals, but such figures are generally considered a fair indication, of the moral standard of a community. I might refer to strikes. It is no use disguising the fact that a strike is an incipient civil war. Strikes have happened in every part of the country, and troops have had to be turned out to preserve order. At the present time the troops are still under arms in British Columbia in order to preserve law and order.
That is a fine state of things under Tory rule.

I want my good friend
to observe that law and order are preserved under Tory rule. However, Sir, iliet uis hope, in regard to this century, ' a bad beginning may bring a good ending.' The ground must be prepared for peace, as an Irishman once said, as well as for potatoes.	You must lay the foundation deep and strong in the hearts and intellects not only of one community, but in all communities, in order to preserve peace. That condition of affairs has not been reached in any country, much less in our country. That is a condition, as Robbie Burns said, that involves two parties:
Nae mon can be at peace unless his neighbour let him.
The condition involves education, culture, gentleness, firmness, self-control, obedience -that is the power or capacity to obey- control or power to command others, responsibility and individuality. These have been defined as the triumph through wisdom and reason of sound principles of human government. Peace is also a condition brought about by the knowledge on the part of those concerned that each party comes of a race who are careful to know and value sacred rights, who will seek every honourable means of settling differences, but who, in case an opponent should be determined to be domineering, unjust, dishonourable or repressive, would know how to defend the honour of home, of loved ones and country, and who, in defence of those sacred heritages, would willingly sacrifice each his own life. The essentials, therefore, of peace are discipline on the part of the

people; training in self-defence; manoeuvring, shooting straight, withstanding fatigue, privations, etc.; stout hearts and stubborn wills; preparedness, arms, equipment, stores, etc. The great peace advocate, who heroically passed away on that awful night amid the icy waters, on the Titantic, Mr. W. T. Stead, said:
When a nation shall have reached the point where every citizen feels it is his duty and privilege to he trained for the defence of the fatherland, it will become a greater, a saner and more efficient people.
That is the aim and object which I have in view, and my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition, I believe, holds similar views. Another prominent writer, Major Stewart L. Murray, said:
A great power cannot escape adequate payment for national defence. It Is not a matter of what we choose to pay. It Is a matter of what we must pay, even in the form of adequate preparation for victory; or later in the form of a war indemnity for defeat.
The country that is overrun or invaded is the country that suffers. While a country that is invaded and devastated undoubtedly suffers much, it is on the other hand an historical fact that it is the country which has not been invaded which eventually comes to the front. I might point out in that regard, to meet the arguments that aTe sometimes advanced, that the gTeat upheavals in literary effort and production <and intellectual development have invariably followed great wars by which, although the invaded countries have been practically ruined for the time being, yet aJll have risen thereafter to hitherto undreamed of heights of literary and intellectual splendour, as instance the Augustan age, the Renaissance, the Elizabethan period and the Reformation. These periods of intellectual activity followed closely upon great wars. Mr. Harold F. Wyatt says:
The discovery that Christianity is incompatible with military spirit is made only among decaying peoples. While a nation is still vigorous, while its population is still expanding, while the blood in its veins is strong, then on this head no scruples are felt. But when its energies begin to wither, wlien self-indulgence takes the place of self-sacrifice, when its sons and daughters become degenerate, then it is that a spurious and bastard humanitarianism masqueradiiig as religion declares war to he an anachronism and a barbarous sin.
Lord Roberts, on the same lines, says:
The dramatic three weeks' campaign which ended in the complete collapse of the Turkish army shows, with a ruthless logic, the effect of apathy and unpreparedness. . . The ghastly accounts of the slaughter that has transformed
Albania into a shambles should surely bring home to us what war in a country may mean to that country. . . The . clays of muddling through a war . . . are over. Bet me implore you, as a soldier of more than fifty years' service, who knows what war was and what it is now, not to be led away by any such dangerous beliefs.
Instance after instance might he quoted to show that countries that have progressed and pr ispered are countries that have ibeen visited by war. The great Maehia-velli said:
All the armed prophets have conquered; all the unarmed have perished.
We have Eliza Cook saying:
Never trust the soft breathing that preaches of Peace.
With a pledge-giving lip and a smile-lighted eye-
Hear it all with good will, but he provident still-*
With men that are earnest and pbwder that's dry.
The German Chancellor recently said:
As long as men are men and States are States, the question of limiting armaments will remain insoluble.
Therefore, I am sorry that I have to fall in with the ranks of those who believe that universal peace is yet far off, and that wars wiir continue to devastate, and that just as eternal vigilance is the price of liberty, so eternal readiness to defend loved ones, home and country, is the price of peace. Ex-President Roosevelt has been more or less laughed at, but nevertheless the old gentleman keeps up his pace through the world and keeps his hat on his head fairly well in spite of the sneers and criticisms of minor intellects. Mr. Roosevelt has been recently oil a trip to South America and he has pointed out that the only two countries where he found anything like a stable form of civilized or constitutional government are Argentina and Chile. He attributes that entirely to the fact that these, two peoples have fairly respectable militia systems and are trained in self-control and self-development. In case of war, the farmers and shippers of this country would lose more in a month than preparedness for war would cost them in a generation. 'My hon. friend (Mr. Devlin) has pointed out the fact that I went on a junket to Virginia recently. I did take a junket through Virginia.

How did you find
it?

I liked it very well, and I would recommend my hon. friend to go. Let me point out that Virginia was the scene of many battles in the great American Civil War, and that while the portions of the country that were actually devastated, where houses were burned and farms destroyed, have not yet recovered their former status, all those parts of the country that were not actually invaded, long, long ago recovered; in fact, their recovery was almost immediate. I read a letter in this House once from a former Canadian resident in New York, pointing out the imperative need of the people of this country being ready to repel any invasion coming from whatever quarter it might, and I agree that it is our duty to maintain such a state of preparedness.
Civilization depends on liberty. There can be no civilization without liberty, no liberty without law and order, no law and order without power-[DOT]

My hon. friend will
excuse me for touching a tender spot. The memories of last night seem still too fresh. These cadet corps were organized on ,a small scale; they were not systematized. We are now endeavouring to systematize them throughout the length and breadth of the country. During the last year we have drilled, equipped and inspected 44,680 cadets, of whom it is estimated that upwards of 30,000 are sixteen years of age and upwards. When I point out that many of the men who fought in the ranks at Alma, especially in the Welsh regiments who fought at Waterloo, who fought during the American war, were sixteen years of age and upwards-Wolfe himself was only .fifteen when he entered the army-it will be seen that boys of sixteen years of age and upwards make very good soldiers, and it will be realized what an asset these cadets are for the defence of the Dominion of Canada. Any commercial traveller in Canada will tell you pretty accurately what towns have cadet corps by the manhood, straightforward, cleanly bearing of the young boys and young ladies in those towns. I have no hesitation in saying that I aspire to raise the character of these boys and girls throughout this Dominion.
What about the province of Quebec?

In the province of Quebec, that everybody is afraid to touch even with a pair of tongs,, we have 16,320 cadets trained in the secondary schools and colleges and senior primary schools. I, a fire-eating Orangeman, inspected 4,800 French-Canadian boys in the city of Montreal, and there were 160 priests there also. These boys are a credit to any country ; and it is my purpose, if I can get away, to go down to Montreal on Saturday with brother John and watch him review 500 boys in one institution there. If any of my hon. friends come along with me, they will see four battalions of cadets in Mont St. Louis college fit to take the field to-morrow and to handle rifles with any ordinary regiment. In addition to this we have trained 12,000 teachers during the last year or two. Our object in training these teachers is that they may take their classes and train them in squad drill. I have seen 1,800 children of five years and upwards, come out of a school and march around, forming two deep and four deep, and scarcely a child out of step. These have all been trained by lady teachers. We believe in training people when they are young, because no man can become a good base-ball player or cricket player or lacrosse player unless he learns the game when he is a boy. When he is grown up, he has not the activity and suppleness of the muscles necessary for the development of perfection in the science. We have a large number of trained teachers in every large centre in Canada to-day; they train the teachers in the schools who in turn train the children, and thus the *country is saved a great deal of expense in not having to send instructors to these places. Since I have assumed office 12,000 have taken cadet certificates, and 17,000 officers and teachers in Canada have been given military certificates. It is unnecessary for me to go into the details. Our instructional staff now numbers 251 persons.
Now, coming to the question of drill-halls It is true we have indulged in the construction of these buildings, and criticism has been made, some kindly and some unkindly. But let me remind hon. members of what Barnum once said-that he spent 375,000 in publishing condemnations of his own show and $750,000 in positively advertising it. And he said: I get ten times the value from the $75,000 than I do from the $750,000, for the condemnation is widely copied and is discussed everywhere, but the advertisement is just the same for nobody pays a particle of attention to the adverse criticism. So, in this drill-hall business, adverse and even unkind criticism only helps the popularity of this policy. Not' more than a thousand years ago certain gentlemen in a political campaign indulged in criticisms of drill-halls, but since the people have had time to settle down to an understanding of the situation the public generally, including the farmers, are becoming strongly

favourable to this policy of drill-halls. Six weeks ago I had a deputation of eighty-five representatives from a town in a farming locality, many of them farmers, asking for a drill-hall. I asked one of these farmers: Why are you interested in this? And he said:	I have my son to think of; why
should he grow up without the opportunity for physical development and training that is afforded to the boys in the towns? Why should not we have some place for Saturdays or week evenings to which our boys could go for drill under the direction of your drill instructor? I want to tell this House and the community at large that in the Militia Department we have applications for over a thousand drill-halls, and we can only supply twenty-five of them this year.

Are these drill-halls for
the general use of the community?
, Mr. HUGHES: I am glad my hon. friend mentioned that point. The policy is to have them primarily for the use of the militia and cadet corps, but they are there for the use of any other organization that wants them for similar purposes. They can be thrown open also for any town gathering where there is no hall-any philanthropic or patriotic meeting, any meeting of a farmers' association and other gatherings of that kind as a friend near me suggests they are there for any laudable public use.
Are they given free?
So far as we are concerned, they are always given free. But I suppose there is a local charge for cleaning them up and that kind of thing.
The hon. minister should have no difficulty in finding places to accept drill halls all over the country, on those conditions.

That is what I want to do if I can get the' money. And I am coming to that in a minute-I will show my hon. friend how we are going to get that money. An hon. gentleman near me asks if these drill halls aie allowed to be used for political purposes. I say, certainly- let them be used by either party. Suppose that in a town there is no suitable ball and this is visited by an ex-minister of the Crown or a member of Parliament who is to deliver an address, why should not he speak in the drill hall? If my hon. friend from Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) comes to my town, for instance, to address the free and independent electors there, he will find the drill hall available for his use.

I might get one of the
hon. minister's automobiles, too.

I should be glad to give the hon. gentleman a ride in mine. But the automobiles of the Militia Department are such cheap ones-$550 and $750-that a gentleman of his position, one accustomed to the $6,000 and $8,000 automobiles, would find it rather beneath his dignity, I fear, to ride in one of ours. The one in which he stuck in the Modder river and where he waived his hand and said: Get out you men from other colonies and pull me out, was one of the high price kind, I assume, so he would hardly be satisfied with the seven hundred dollar automobile which the Minister of Militia is content to use.
Let me point out that since Confederation in Canada, drill halls have cost the tremendous sum of $4,900,000 all told. In the fifty years, almost, of the Canadian Confederation, the whole cost of drill halls has been less than $5,000,000. Another important matter which we have before the department is the training of officers. In order to secure a splendid lot of officers in the service we have developed officers' training corps in connection with the universities and some of the larger institutions of the land. In connection with McGill university, Lord Strathcona, before his death, handed over a sum of nearly $100,000 wherewith to purchase a site for a drill hall adjacent to McGill university. There is an officers' training corps in connection with McGill University. Canon Dauth of Laval University, Montreal, has already organized five companies. These companies are made up of 450 of the students who are training for law, medicine, and the professions. He promised me that before the end of the year he would have 800 or 900 in training. In connection with Queen's University, I might say that an old friend of that institution-a	distinguished graduate of the Royal Military College and an engineer of note-has presented Queen's University with ground on which the Government is supposed to erect a drill hall. He has also presented ground on which to erect residence buildings. Altogether, it is costing him $600,000 of his own money. That is the spirit that is abroad in the community to-day. Laval, McGill, Queen's, Dalhousie, the British Columbia University, Sackville University-the president of which, I may say, came all the way to Ottawa in connection with organizing an officers' training corps-Toronto, Manitoba, and Edmonton-all these universities are making arrangements for the establishment of officers' training corps. They have found the effect of discipline on the students so splendid that they are going more and more into it in the future. These young gentlemen will go out into the country as lawyers, doctors, leading business men-they will be educated gentlemen, at all events-and although maybe having no intention of becoming military men, they will gravitate towards some military company, and the country will have the benefit of their services. That is my policy in connection with university officers' training corps. It costs the country very little. There is no harm in my mentioning that Colonel Leonard is the gentleman who is

making that gilt to Queen's University. The students will reside in the buildings he will erect, and the Government will pay just what we would pay at our schools of instruction. We will furnish the instructors, and the country will get the benefit of the services of these young gentlemen of the best calibre. We also hold classes for those men in the villages throughout the country who are so busy that they cannot take the time to go to camp, and an officer or sergeant goes down to those localities and puts the men into shape, so that we are getting all the practical benefit of schools at a minimum of expense. We have also musketry schools all over the country where officers are trained in the art of teaching the rudiments of musketry. We have also cadet instructors, and the Royal Military College, as usual, is doing splendid work. There is another matter to which I have given a little attention, and which has been more or less belittled by our friends opposite-for what reason I do not know. It is not always the man who wears a uniform that becomes a great warrior. Clive, Nicholson, Lawton, Wood of the United States army, were all civilians. General Wood was a doctor, and a doctor is not generally expected to be a great waTrior. Many of the best soldiers in history were civilians. Stonewall Jackson was a university professor.
You are a civilian yourself.

Certainly; that is the very point I am making. Some gentlemen say you cannot have a democratic army. I admit that you cannot have a democratic standing army, but you can have a democratic militia. If it is properly trained from the earliest years of school life, and the training is carried on afterwards, there is no reason why you should not have a democratic army, the equal, if not the superior, of any standing army in the world.

Coming now to the active militia,. I may say that the active militia is divided into two classes, the permanent corps and the non-permanent, the permanent corps consisting of 3,021 officers and men and the non-permanent force consisting of 74,606 officers and men. We hear a great deal about militarism in Canada. I have never been an advocate of a permanent or standing army except for instructional purposes. I am reducing the permanent force. I inherited, in the permanent force, an army service corps which was in size 25 per cent of the army service corps that the whole of the British army has. I am reducing that. I am putting men in other employment and I have made up my mind that I will not have a large number of men in our army service corps about the country. The danger to the country is from the permanent end of the military forces, not the non-permanent end. In the permanent service men are taken out of continuous em-

pioyment, they are taken from the other services of the country and they become a special and privileged class while the great majority of the people are untrained. Under these circumstances people are like men standing around the edge of a football field-mere rooters watching the regulars go by. With a permanent army, in a time of crisis in the nation's history, there is danger, unless the officers are constitutionally trained, of the officers and men obeying the mandate of some oligarchic government, autocratic Upper House, or Divine right ruler.
What do you mean by that ?

My hon. friend can read and he can exercise his intellectual powers. In olden times home training fitted men for the army. To-day it does not. In olden times every boy could handle the quarter-staff and the single stick. To-day the service is very different; the sword is no more used, but the long-range rifle in the hands of the straight shooter is what counts. We must have the militia spirit if we want to have a proper militia sys-! tem, because we could not, in a country such as Canada, afford to maintain a large standing army. The non-permanent militia of the country represent the people at large. It is file right and duty oi every citizen to demand to be trained. Counting corps organized and those asking to be equipped, we have 78,000 men. There is a regiment in Hull, 'another in Maison-neuve, another in Sault Ste. Marie, another in Toronto, and regiments all over Canada, organized and officers selected for them, but we have not the armament, the equipment or the money to enable them to be trained. There are cavalry regiments waiting. There is a regiment in Prince Edward Island, and there are regiments in other places, but we have not the equipment which would be required to put men into harness. Otherwise, instead of having 78,000, I would have 150,000 men and 40,000 cadets. It is the right of every citizen to demand to be trained, and it is the right of every government to meet the citizens, in so far as possible, in their demand to be trained. friend will explain for wha/t reason the officers went over?

That is four drill halls. In 1912-13, the first year I was in office, this jumped up to $44,707; but every officer who was sent bad been picked and billed to go by my predecessor and I carried out the
bill. I shall tell you how I showed my loyalty to my predecessor as I would to any man whom I succeeded. One officer had stood at the polls at Halifax and had turned all the votes he could from my right hon. leader (Mr. Borden), had canvassed against him and got men out of the way whom he could not influence against him.
I should have dismissed the fellow from the force. I did not do it, he was a good officer.

Slow torture.

I brought him to
Ottawa. He saw his mistake and I forgave him, but I sent him back to his regiment. He was a good officer but a foolish misguided fellow in politics. He was brought before me, I showed him his error and sent him back to his regiment. I found out that he was one of those billed to go to England, and although the department had been largely loaded up by friends of the Administration of hon. gentlemen opposite, I sent that fellow .to England to take his course, and his expenses form part of the $44,000 rolled up here. The next year, 1913-14, I changed the programme and the cost of sending officers to England was reduced to $10,000. These officers went over from the permanent force. I am not saying one word against the permanent force. The officers are splendid fellows as a rule, tip-top fellows; but I want the House to understand that the Dominion of Canada has too long educated these men. The farmers and taxpayers of Canada have been educating the permanent officers for a good many years. We send them to the schools, we take them in as novices, we send them for the long course in England. I claim that this course could be as well administered here and accordingly we brought out

for my predecessor had adapted this plan and we carried it on-we brought out officers for especially training these men. We let the officers who are being trained carry on their work in the regiment in the ordinary service at the same time that they were

taking their instru'ctiion and in this way we saved money. The permanent force in Canada are but a handful, some three thousand, many of them are utilized as servants. The officers, nice young fellows, would not officer more than a couple of regiments. The men who would have to do the fighting, who have done the fighting, are largely the nonpermanent officers and non-permanent men of this country. I looked around from the Atlantic to the Pacific, I saw men of worth, education, stand and culture like my hon. friend from Woodstock, N.B. (Mr. Carvell), and myself and a lot more of us who had given their time, energy and skill for years-
I am not in your class.

I was going to bring you up to my level. I could give the names of officers who have spent $50,000 on their regiments, and who annually spend $5,000 to $10,000 on the militia. Lawyers, doctors, teachers, farmers, business men, and preachers-for we get some of them-are the men who officer the militia of this country. I made up my mind that the young permanent corps fellows, splendid boys though they he, were not going to be the only ones to have an opportunity of studying the militia of other lands. The first year I had a chance, I sent over seven officers and two non-commissioned officers to the British manoeuvres. The success of the experiment was splendid. The cost was $6,800, and they watched the British and French manoeuvres for weeks. In 1913-14, sixteen non-permanent officers and five permanent officers went over at a cost of $24,620.33-two drill-halls and a half. They saw the British manoeuvres, the French and the Swiss manoeuvres. The officers who went over were chosen from all parts of Canada, regardless of politics. There was, I tjiink, one more Grit than Tory in the party.
Did you go to Belgium?
Yes, personally.

I do not know what the hon. gentleman means.
Were you recognized as British officers?

They knew we were
Canadians, but of course my hon. friend is aware that the arrangements were made through the British authorities.

We are British officers, although we are Canadians. I am a British officer. We were received with the utmost courtesy. I might point out that at these foreign manoeuvres only two officers are allowed in uniform from each country, and the rest go in mufti.
I am told that my hon. friend was taken for Kitchener.

I take that as a compliment; I certainly was not taken for the Emperor of Japan. The officers owed much to the kindness of General French, General Hamilton and General Ellison. General Ellison was a very old friend to the Swiss and his kindness made the way smooth for us. Every officer from Canada received the most courteous treatment everywhere, I am glad to say.
In regard to Switzerland, I have been studying with a great deal of interest the militia system of that country for the past two years. In that country the service is obligatory and universal. There are three classes: the Elite, comprised of men between twenty and thirty-two years of age; the Landwehr, thirty-three to forty years; and the Landsturm, forty-one to forty-eight years. The administration is partly by cantons, and partly by the Confederation. There is a non-training tax. I want to emphasize that point. Every man, rich or poor, who does not train has to pay 6 francs a year, and an additional li francs for each 1,000 francs of net property and 100 francs net income. In 1911 the Swiss people paid 44,777,894.15 francs towards the militia out of a total expenditure of 172,439,221 francs. That is in Confederation taxes alone.	The amount spent on the militia represents 26 per cent of the total expenditure of the country. The rifle ranges, and organizations of that sort, are paid for by the cantons. The total force in 1911 was 408,600,851; made up of 142,054 men in the Elite; 69,513 in the Landwehr; 68,579 in the Landsturm; and 206,705 in the Complementary. I think the oath of the Swiss soldier will stand repeating:
L,e serment de fidfilitfi au drapeau est prete selon la foririule suivante:
'Les officiers, sous-offlclers ou soldats jurent ou promettent solennellement:
'He rester fidSles 8, la Confederation; de sacrifler leur vie pour la defense de la patrie et de sa constitution; de ne jamais abandonner les drapeaux; de se conformer strictement aux lois militaires; d'obeir scrupuleusement et ponctuellement aux ordres de leurs chefs; de maintenir et d'observer une discipline severe et de faire tout ce que l'honneur et la liberte de la patrie exigent d'eux.'

In passing, I might say that all the officers who went over to the British manoeuvres were men of high standing in their local communities. Since their return they have given, regularly, lectures to the various corps in the country-a thing never done before, and in that way the whole militia is getting the benefit of their experience at the foreign manoeuvres.
The Dominion arsenal has been revised. Without going into details, I might say we found defects in the ammunition. Accidents were occurring all the time, and two of the very best experts were brought over from the war office to look over the arsenal. In brief, their report was as follows: No adequate inspection; twelve million rounds of rifle ammunition was ordered to he destroyed as unfit; eighteen-pounder quickfiring ammunition was found to be defective, the loss on these eighteen-pounders amounting to $100,000; there was no cordite for 6 months during which time bullets and cases were made; seven thousand eighteen-pounder shells had been completed, and 20,000 partly so, but only one was found to be properly shaped; 75 were selected for the firing test, lEj of which would not enter the gun at all; one burst within the gun and nearly spoiled it-a $7,000 gun. New dies and machinery have been put in and the very best ammunition is now being turned out. I would ask the House to call it six o'clock. I wish to thank hon. gentlemen very much for their patience.

[Mr. Carvell.J
