I think the hon. member will search i*n vain the annals of this House for the record of any man who has been more ready to furnish information and data to his opponents than myself. During the three years that I have been presenting the Militia Estimates, the items were sent out every time to every; hon. member in advance, so that they could have the fullest opportunity of getting posted as to the facts.
My hon. friend is in error. The same course was pursued by his predecessor.
In general, not in detail. I have all the reports.
There was a document of some kind.
Yes, a general document, but my information was sent out in detail, giving every vote.
That is a matter of degree.

Yes, but I sent out the information, showing that I was anxious to inform the House and the country as to the matters of my department. I have come here and shown frankly that I endorsed every vote that Sir Frederick Borden asked for. I am not finding fault with that; I have brought this matter up merely to show that, no matter who was in charge of the Militia Department, these accounts had to be paid.
The minister has indeed been vetry generous in answering questions, but the complaint of the hon. member for Prescott is a rather personal one and I think the minister should give it his attention.

If it is a personal
matter, let the hon. member come to me personally and I will talk to him.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I must remind hon. members that the rule is that the point of order or objection to any word must be taken immediately upon its being spoken.
I myself did not hear the word, but the 216
rule as laid down by Bourinot is as I have said and I rule accordingly.

I put a fair question to the minister this afternoon; I will put it to him again and I hope he will answer it. He was speaking about the travelling expenses of iSir Ian Hamilton and himself last summer and, he was comparing them with the expenses of the trip of Sir John French. I asked him whether ot not he travelled with Sir Ian Hamilton in a special train and he declined to answer my question. Will the minister answer the question now?
Sir Ian Hamilton travelled with me in a special train.
How much did the hon. gentleman pay for that special train?

I gave the figures this
afternoon.
The figures were given in a lump sum; I would like to know what was the cost of this special train?

The figures have been
given two or three times during this session, in answer to questions.
Can the minister not give me the information now?
I will get the information for the hon. gentleman when we take up the item.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am confronted with a difficult question. I would like to know whether it is the desire of the committee to have a general discussion, or whether we shall proceed item by item.

Having given my general statement this afternoon, I am now ready to be interrupted just as often as hon. gentlemen desire to ask questions. I will endeavour to answer their questions, as I have always done, frankly and squarely, with no turning corners and with no equivocation whatever.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I must insist on having the decision of the committee, because I am in a difficult position. The rule says that speeches in Committee of the Whole must be strictly relevant to the item or clause under discussion.

Would it not be a very grave error on the part of this committee to depart from the rule which has been adhered to, according to my recollection, for the last ten years? The rule has always



been in our book of rules, but we have never been absolutely confined to the single item under discussion. A wide range of discussion is allowed, and I do not think the Minister of Militia will take the ground that tve are to be absolutely bound down to the item under discussion.

Last year and other
years there was always a great deal of rambling over almost everything.

I do not think we should have this as a matter of grace or favour from the minister. We do not want any favours from this minister, conversation in the corridor used in public addresses to the contrary notwithstanding. I do not wish to reflect upon your action in raising the point, Mr. Chairman, but it seems to me to be very strange that it should be necessary to have the decision of the committee formally declared in this matter when the wide discussion of Estimates has been the custom, to my knowledge, for nine sessions. If the Chair were anxious to comply with the rules, would it not have been more in order to say: have we the unanimous consent of the committee to go on with these Estimates to-day, it being Thursday, and the Estimates not having been previously taken up? I wish to place myself on record as contending that we have the right, according to custom almost from time immemorial in this House, to ask the minister at the opening of his Estimates any question with regard to the expenditures of his department,

I asked the minister some questions in connection with the renting or purchasing of property in Sherbrooke from Mrs. A. N. Worthington, and I got the reply that the property was leased at a rental of $100 a month and was being used for temporary quarters. For what purpose are those quarters to be used ?

As the hon. member knows, the armoury part of the drill hall of the 53rd regiment is not yet ready. The old court house is to be fitted up for that purpose, and in the meantime the officers, non-commissioned officers and band must have other quarters. These rooms have been rented for that purpose.
Are the men going to drill there ?
They are to. have their lectures and meetings there, the same as they do in drill halls.

Are these premises to be used, according to military terms, as an

officers' mess, or what I would call an officers' club ? For what purpose are they to be used ?

In every drill hall
in Canada they have rooms for the purpose of holding meetings, lectures and so on, and where the drill hall does not provide that accommodation, we rent premises outside. They are used by the officers for lecture purposes, for examination purposes, for studying and, I presume, for conversation and smoking.

The St. George's Club building was burned last fall, and the club moved into this building and are now, or were until lately, occupying it. Have any arrangements been made with the St. George's club to remain there, and if so, on what terms ?
I understand that the club has given notive to vacate the premises and allow the officers to take charge.
How soon ?
I do not know the details, but I can find out.

My information from people in Sherbrooke is that the members of the St. George club are to remain there as the guests of the officers of the 53rd regiment until such time as they have rebuilt their own building. Is that correct ?

I have never heard
of it, but I will look into the matter.
When was this building rented from Mrs. Worthington ?

Very recently; within
the last few weeks.
Permit me to ask again whether or not these premises are to be used for what is called in military terms an officers' mess ?
It is used identically for the same purposes as similar rooms are used in drill halls: for the holding of meetings and for any legitimate purpose in connection with the regiment.

This building, I believe, has been used as an officers' mess, or officers' club. It is also used, and has been since last December, by the St. George's Club, and I understand and believe they are still occupying it. My information was they were invited to remain there as guests of the 53rd Regiment until they had rebuilt their own building.

I am not jealous of this, nor do I think the recompense is more than the St. ,George's Club deserves, for I think they are worthy of nearly everything the Conservative party can do for them, because that institution has been a Conservative committee room ever since I knew anything about it, and I assume it is yet. But -what I am a little inquisitive about is whether it is necessary to have a place of this kind or not. We have two drill-hal'ls in the city of Sherbrooke, and a good deal of military equipment. I am inclined to think that the expenditure of public money for an officers' club is not quite the best use of public money, even for military purposes. I think the people of the county of Sherbrooke will tell you so when the proper time comes. The city of Sherbrooke has a population of less than 20,000. We have two pretty expensive drill-halls, as I have said, one with a complete armoury, and the other is to have an up-to-date armoury in every respect. Now, militarism may be a good thing, but I do not know that a population of nearly
20,000	needs two drill-halls. Besides these, the militia occupy two other buildings. In the Brooks block, they are using the upper stories, as well as an apartment downstairs, for which they pay $75 per month, and they rent this property from Mrs. Worthington, for which they pay $100 per month. I think that public money could be spent to better advantage. If, for instance, the same amount were devoted to teaching the people how to farm properly, it would serve a better purpose than spending it on militarism. I am not inclined to find a great deal of fault politically, because I think this will do more good to me than to the party it was intended to help. But politics is not a thing in which I make my living nor is it a thing in which I am much interested. My business here is to give the Government my advice and opinion; and my advice and opinion is that it would be well for the Prime Minister to pay a little attention to the militia administration.
The Minister of Militia, this afternoon, referring to an answer I had made to him, said that I had just woke up. Perhaps I have; and perhaps I have taken longer to wake up than I ought. But I think he will find that a lot of other people have waked up, and are waking up. They say that a word to the wise is sufficient; and I will just take the minister into my confidence to the extent of telling him that I do 216J
not think his militarism is quite as popular in the county of Sherbrooke as he believes it to be. I would advise him to go slow and be careful. The minister also said that it was a necessary part of the training of young men to teach them to shoot straight in case of trouble. I do not know whether the people who attend that club will be able to shoot straight when the time comes or not. My impression is they will not.
The hon member has proven himself a veritable warrior-blackguarding the St. George's club behind their backs.
Oh, oh.
I know nothing about it; never knew there was -such a dub in existence, and do not know it yet.

I rise to a point of order. I ask whether if i't is in order even for a minister of the Crown to say that an hon. member of this House ' blackguards ' anybody. And if that expression is unparliamentary I ask that the minister be commanded to take it back.
Mr. Chairman-
Chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The minister has a
right to speak to the point of order.
I did not charge any man with blackguarding-
What did you say?

The hon. gentleman
can find that out from the ' Hansard '. The hon. member has seen fit to take a certain course-

The hon. minister can speak to the point of order, but he cannot speak on other matters until the Chair has ruled. My point is this:	That the Minister of Militia did say of the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. McCrea) that he had blackguarded the St. George's, club behind their backs.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Do I understand that the words have been used?
You heard what I said.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I am afraid the word ' blackguard ' applied to any hon. member of this House is pretty strong language. It is better that it should not be used in this House.

Some lion. MEMBERS: Withdraw. Take it back.
I have not used the *word with reference to any member of this House.

I ask your ruling, Mr. Chairman. I say that in my hearing the hon. minister used the expression in^ regard to the hon. member for Sherbrooke ' blackguarding the St. George's club behind their backs '.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The minister had better explain what he meant and to whom he applied the word. If the word was applied to the hon. member, I must repeat, it should not be used in this House and should be taken back.
Chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I understand the minister says he did not apply the word to the hon. member.
He did.

My point of order is- But I see the minister has risen, does he wish to speak to the point of order?
Mr. HUGHES': I am not speaking to a point of order.

Then, I am not through with it, Mr. Chairman. It is not enough for you to rule that the expression should be withdrawn, but it is your duty to compel its withdrawal. If a member commits a breach of parliamentary decorum, he cannot evade or escape the ruling of the Chair by saying that he did not say what every member heard him say. As he has used the expression-as you heard him use it- it is not only your duty to rule it out of order as unparliamentary, but it is equally and imperatively your duty to command him to take it back.

May I be allowed to analyse briefly what the minister said. Perhaps ihe does not have a full appreciation of the significance of the language he used and, I say that in all charity. What we heard on this side was a charge on the part of the minister that the hon. member for Sherbrooke had blackguarded the St. George's club of his town of Sherbrooke-

Behind their
backs.	'

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: There is a rule"which says that whatever a member says in explanation, whether relating to the words or to the meaning of his speech, is to be taken as true and not afterwards called into question. It is true that I have heard the word ' blackguard,* but the fact that the minister said that he did not apply the word to the hon. member falls under this rule, and I think even if it could be interpreted in the way some members interpret it, it can be taken as having been taken back.

The hon. member has referred to the renting of these halls. He knows as well as any one that there are two regiments in Sherbrooke, and he knows as well as any one the cause of the difficulty that has arisen in the city of Sherbrooke. One is a very excellent French-Canadian regiment.
What was your ruling, Mr. Chairman?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I ruled that the hon. minister having declared that he did not apply the words to the hon. member for Sherbrooke, the point of order is settled.
To whom did he apply them ?

I have been listening
attentively, and I have not yet heard the minister say that he did not apply these words to the hon. member for Sherbrooke.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The question is settled.

I think the minister has almost attempted to deny having used these words. We all know he did use them. His friends behind him as well as	members on this side
know that he did use the words. If the minister wants to make an explanation according to your ruling, and say that he did not apply them to the member for Sherbrooke, possibly he would have the right to do so. I feel that we ought to have this matter settled, and the minister has no

more right in this House than a common member. Surely the minister does not want to transgress the rules of debate. I think it is his duty to explain exactly what he did mean by the word he used.
I have stated that I did not apply the words to the hon. member for Sherbrooke, and that ends the matter as far as I am concerned.
To whom did you apply them?

I am not called upon
to say.
On the point of order-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I consider that the point of order is settled.
No; I have the right to appeal; but before appealing-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: It is perfectly in order to appeal-

Before appealing, I wish to ask the Prime Minister, who is regarded on this side of the House as in every way a perfect gentleman, if he will give to us an expression of his opinion as to the propriety of the language used by his Minister of Militia with regard to the hon.- member for Sherbrooke. The Prime Minister is responsible for the decorum in this House and I ask him, partly out of kindness for the Minister of Militia himself, to give us an expression of his opinion of that language.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: As I understood the Minister of Militia he said he did not apply any such expression to any hon. member in this House.
Did you believe him.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
My hon. friend knows
that the significance of the words of any member of this House must be taken according to his intention as declared. He has declared that he did not apply any such expression or intend to apply any such expression to any hon. member in this House.
Why did he use it?
The Prime Minister has not told us all he thinks about it.

The member for Sherbrooke (Mr. McCrea) knows the reason for th'e new regiment there. One is French-
Canadian and the other is English. The 53rd had no drill-hall, they were occupying the drill-hall in the French-Canadian end of the town and in order to get rid of the difficulty created not by me but by my predecessor-I do not know whether my hon. friend -was instrumental in having the matter arranged-at all events it was done under the rule of my predecessor the French-Canadian regiment, the 54th, a very excellent regiment, was placed at the upper end of the town in the new drill hall. The 53rd were going to occupy it at certain times until their own drill-hall would be ready. Their own drill-hall was not ready, and the armouries, as the hon. gentleman knows, were not ready. They had good quarters in the old drill-hall. It would have been unfair to have asked them to leave this old drill-hall, to give up the rooms where the officers held their meetings and go uptown where they 'had no rooms to go to. In other words, the department having moved them out of the old drill-hall, had to put them into the armouries where they would have offices. These are the offices fOT the new regiment, the 53rd and it is the intention to occupy these until the old building has been placed in a condition to be used as offices for the 53rd Regiment. The hon. member knows that as well as any one and I fail to see the motive for his action to-night. I have never heard, of any other purpose until to-night.

I might say to the Minister of Militia that the people of the Eastern Townships are surprised at the minister, after saying that he is abolishing liquor in all camps throughout this Dominion, allowing his officers to have rooms in the St. George's Club and pay rent for same. The St. George's Club is known in the city of Sherbrooke as a Tory organization. The minister says that he does not know what the St. George's Club is. I am surprised that he would come before this House of intelligent men and make such a statement. In the city of Sherbrooke, as the minister has explained, there are two large drill-halls built at a very large expense. After the St. George's Club was burned last fall, they rented the premises of Mrs. Worthington. I suppose they found it hard to keep up the expense and they asked the minister to help bear the expense. In that club they serve something besides cold water. The minister knows it and if he does not he should know it. Two years ago the minister was down in the city of Sherbrooke. Will he say he did not go to-the St. George's Club?
[DOT]3426
I went to some club and had a luncheon; I do not know where it was.

And you know whether they served some whisky blanc there. I am surprised when the minister says he did not know that there was such a club. Now he has to admit it.
Mr. SAM. HUGHES: The hon. member has put words in my mouth that I did not use. I never heard of the St. George's in my life before to-night, and I never knew that liquor was sold in the club. I presume that, following the custom of clubs throughout Canada, liquor may be sold in it. I am not running the clubs, I am running the militia of Canada. When the officers rent a building I can assure the House that we look after it, and if there is any such condition of affairs, if the St. George's Club is using the quarters of the 53rd Regiment, inquiry will be made and action will be taken.

Will the minister say that they have not rooms enough in the two drill-halls in Sherbrooke for the accommodation of both battalions? Or is it just for a gentlemen's mess? We do not want that in the Eastern Townships. We are willing to spend a certain amount on the militia, but we are not willing to have the minister pay out money to have gentlemen's clubs. I am -surprised. I understood the Minister of Militia to be working always for the interests of the militia and a lot of our young men in the Eastern Townships do not approve of such action as this.
Mr. MeCREA:	The minister says that
Mrs. Worthington's property has been rented for offices for the 53rd. Is he aware that the upper flat in the Brooks block, which was rented by the department some time before Mrs. Worthington's property, would make splendid offices? That upper flat was used as the city hall of Sherbrooke up to within a couple of years ago, and answered the purpose very well. They had all the room they wanted. The minister would have us believe that Mrs. Worthington's property is used not for an officers' mess, but for offices where the men can transact their business.
Mr. SAM. HUGHES: I do not know what the Brooks block is. We have two apartments in the city of Sherbrooke. One is where the non-commissioned officers have their classes, 'and the other is for the 
officers. If the hon. member knows of any more buildings we have in Sherbrooke I woull like to know it. I remember distinctly that these buildings were rented only temporarily.
Until what time?
Until our other quarters are ready.
When will that be?
During this year, I hope.
If liquor is sold there will you stop paying rent?

Not at all. I may as well tell the House that liquor is not used in camps of instruction. This is not a camp of instruction, but if I find the use of liquor, which was tolerated by my predecessors from time immemorial, being abused by the officers in any drill-hall they will quickly walk out of that building.

The minister knows that
the St. George's club is in the same building.
I do not know anything about it.

I can vouch for it. One of the militia men told me that the St. George's club serves whisky, and all kinds of liquor. They have a, good time there and I do not blame them, but I do not think it is right that the department should pay $100 a month rent for those rooms. Now that the minister knows that the St. George's club occupies part of that building I think he should see to it that the officers leave the building.
Mr. SAM. HUGHES: I have already assured the House that I know nothing whatever about any club, and the House may rest assured that if we find any liquor being used excessively or improperly in the buildings we pay rent for, it shall be stopped immediately; but in the first place I shall require some evidence, and at the present time I have no evidence of it whatever.
Who rented this building, and who is it rented from?
The building was rented on petition of the officers I expect through Colonel Denison, the commanding officer. It was rented from Mrs. Worthington.

Does the minister mean to tell me that Mrs. Worthington, who had already rented that property to the St. George's Club, who are now occupying the building, would rent it over again to the department without saying anything about it?

I know nothing about
it further than that the building was asked for by our officers, and that Mrs. Worthington wrote a letter requesting the department to take the building. The building was rented in the ordinary Tegular way.
Did not the minister state some time ago that he had not only rented that building, but bought it from Mrs. Worthington?
Never.

I am surprised at the minister saying that. He told some gentlemen who asked him about it the other day that his department had bought it. I have no objections to him buying it, but what I do object to is that the minister should allow his officers to remain in the same building as the St. George's Club, after he has been going up and down this country trying to catch votes from the temperance . people by saying that he will not allow whisky to be sold in canteens. I think it is about time the minister should be shown up in his true colours. At two meetings I attended in the Eastern Townships, I heard the hon. minister's friends making a point of that, and trying to catch the votes of the temperance people. The minister surely remembers going to Sherbrooke in 1912, during the provincial election campaign, and promising some of the electors that he would build a drill-hall there if they would elect his friend. The people, however, elected a good Liberal, and the minister's friend was defeated. The minister went to the St. George s Club then, and he knows that they are serving not only white whisky, but different kinds of wine.

If the hon. member means to say that I visited Srerbrooke in connection with a provincial election, he is stating what is deliberately untrue. Does the hon. member mean to say that I took part in that provincial election? If he does, he is stating something for which there is absolutely no foundation.
Do you want me to answer that question?

Moreover, I never saw
liquor at any club in Sherbrooke. I. had dinner at a club there one day-I do not know whether it was the St. George's club or not-tout there was no liquor used in my presence on that occasion.

We had a provincial election in the province of Quebec in May, 1912, and shortly before that election the hon. minister visited Sherbrooke. He promised them almost everything if they would elect his friend. I do not know if he came down purposely to take part in the provincial election, but he was there and made those promises at that time. He went to St. George's club, and then he stated to-night that he did not know what St. George's club was. I do not want to insinuate that the minister took too much whisky blanc, but I know they had some there, and he knows it, too.
Mr. SAM. HUGHES: I was not there at night.

I would like to throw some light on St. George's club. I do not think the hon. member for Richmond and Wolfe (Mr. Tobin) has any right to throw slurs on the members of St. George's club. They are just as respectable people as exist in the eastern townships. There are in almost every club, for the use of its members, wines and liquors, and every member of this House knows it; but there is no liquor in St. George's club for distribution or for sale, or for any visitors to go in and partake of unless it is at the invitation of a member of the club. The house that was owned by Mrs. Worthington has been rented by St. George's club since the time of the burning down of the St. George's club house. As far as I know, it is still occupied, or partially occupied, by St. George's club. I think they intend to use it for the officers of the 53rd. I repeat that the members of St. George's club are as respectable a body of people as live in the Eastern Townships.

I have not said that the members of St. George's club are not respectable. I can tell my hon. friend from Compton (Mr. Cromwell) that I was a member of that club for about ten years, and that I resigned last January. I knew what they served there, and it is a respectable place to go to. But when we have a

Minister of Militia who goes from one end of the country to the other preaching temperance, receiving telegrams of congratulation, addressing the temperance ladies throughout the Dominion, and having him pass resolutions commending him for his pronounced determination to stop the sale of wines and liquors in the canteens at the summer drill camps, when he goes down to the city of Sherbrooke and leases as officers' quarters this club in which they serve all kinds of wines and liquors, and when he comes back here and says he does not know anything about St. George's club, I think it is about time that the people should know it. He is sailing under false colors. I have no objection to a man taking a drink of -whisky. The hon. member for Compton cannot say that St. George's club is not known to be a pretty good Tory organization. That is why I resigned from it.

It is not worth while pursuing the matter any further. I do not mean to say that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Tobin) is deliberately making a statement that he knows to be untrue, but he states what is absolutely without foundation when he says that I was at this club and saw-liquor used there. Even if such were the ease, it would not be my place, when I was a guest at a public institution, to interfere. I have nothing to do with St. George's club, I never heard of it and was never associated with it. We have rented a building for the officers, but St. George's club has nothing to do with it that I am aware of and if it is found that there are any civilians using that club all I can say is that they will very soon cease using it.

The hon. member for Compton, imagining the minister to be very innocent, must have rented the building for the minister's department without telling him anything about St. George's club being there. I hope the minister will see to it that his officers move from the building.

The hon. member for Richmond and Wolfe has stated that I must have rented the building occupied by St. George's club for the minister. If I had rented the building for the minister it would have been perfectly right, because I could rent a building as well as any man from the Eastern Townships. But I want to repudiate the insinuation of the hon. gentleman that the St. George's club was an institution which sold liquor. I have been in St. George's club a great many times and I have never seen such a thing take place 
there in my life. When I said that St. George's club was as respectable a club as was to be found in tre Eastern Townships I was speaking of the present time; I was not going back to the resignation of any member of the club.
If the hon. gentleman says that he did not know that they served any liquor at that club, he was not there at the time.

It is the custom of clubs all over Canada to sell liquor. The leader of the Liberal Opposition in Ontario, who, I believe, is a distinguished temperance man for political purposes, is a member of the Ontario club, which sells liquor.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: President of it.

The minister has just
referred to the leader of the Opposition in the province of Ontario. True it is he belongs to the Ontario club where liquor is sold but I do not believe that even the minister wilt stand in his place and say that Mr. Rowell is anything but a most consistent temperance man.
9 p.m. Some hon. MEMBERS: Oh, oh.
( Mr- PARDEE. Hon. gentlemen may say oh, oh,' but there is no one who can say that N. W. Rowell is not a most consistent temperance man or one who does not live up to the tenets -that he preaches to a degree that perhaps no other man in public life in Canada does to-day. The Minister of Militia has opened up a discussion here upon the militia question in Canada. And he has opened it very widely. He has asked us to come and we are here. He has given us a statement as to how the militia expenditure has been carried on since 1911. I think that hon. members on both sides of the House will agree that from the 'beginning to the end of the minister's remarks they breathe nothing but militancy. It was fight from the beginning, it was fight to the end. You would have thought that the people of Canada were an absolutely warlike people looking for war and trouble instead of devoting themselves to the arts of peace. There was nothing about beating the sword into the ploughshare with the Minister of Militia. With him it was to sharpen the sword on the grindstone and to find a head to cut off and let it fall into -the basket. His attitude was: where is the man who will knock that chip off my shoulder and let Canada and the empire go for him! The minister has several times devoured

Germany almost before breakfast. The latest thing to which he has turned his attention and that of the Militia Department is the eating up of Ireland and all those who do not believe in her cause. Ever since the year 1911, when the Conservative party came into power and when the hon. minister took over the management of the Militia Department-and I say it in all honesty and sincerity-the Minister of Militia has not been as hoping to build up a militia which may be and which ought to be useful; he has been simply building up a militia which may be called out for war at any minute. His idea is absolutely wrong and it is not a good idea for the young people of Canada to grow up with.
I am in favour of the militia; but a minister, who is in charge of the Militia Department of the Dominion of Canada, and who is building up a militia day in and day out along the lines that perhaps to-morrow we shall be at war with somebody, has not got the right idea in mind and is imbuing the spirit of war into the souls of the people of this Dominion. There is no question about the necessity of a militia; but why we should expend on militia the enormous sums that we are expending to-day, is more than I can understand. Canada is a young and growing country, and "we need the $14,000,000 that the minister purposes spending upon militia in the year 1914-5 more for the development of this country than for the purposes to which the Minister of Militia intends putting it.
I would like to give a few figures to the House to show how much has been spent upon the militia since 1911. The hon. Minister of Militia practically stated this afternoon that the people of Canada were quite willing to be taxed for militia expenditures and to be taxed liberally. I take absolute issue with him upon that point. The people of Canada are perfectly willing and satisfied that they should be taxed to a moderate degree in so far as militia expenditures are concerned; but I believe the people have shown that they are not content that they should be taxed to the extent that the Minister of Militia is taxing them to-day. The hon. minister this afternoon compared the expenditures of his predecessor, Sir Frederick Borden, with his own expenditures since 1911. I was unable to follow his argument. Perhaps it was due to my own denseness, but by some subtle jugglery of figures he showed that there was a difference of only $4,000,000 between himself and his predecessor.
In my favour.
Let us see whether that statement holds good. I have a list of the expenditures upon the militia from 1896 to 1911. During that period the total expenditure by the Liberal Government was $63,134,120.
What was the expenditure in 1896?

$2,478,179. The total
expenditure in 1911, the last year of Liberal rule, was $7,009,822, and the total expenditure under thei Liberal rule from 1896 to 1911, fifteen years, was $63,134,120, the total expenditure of the hon. Minister of Militia under this Conservative Government from 1911 to the year 1914, three years, was $43,102,987.
Is the hon. member counting 1910-1911 as the last year of the Liberal Administration, or is he counting that the Liberals are responsible for the expenditure in 1911-1912?

I am counting 1910-1911, and 1911 with $7,009,822, as the last year of Liberal expenditure. The figures for
1914-1915 are as follows:
Main Estimates	$10,845,400
Supplementary Estimates	 339,975
Statutory pay to military members of Militia Council and Inspector
General	 21,000
Items in Public Works Estimates to be spent on drill halls, armouries, etc	 2,355,000
Total	$13,561,375
The hon. Minister of Militia says that his expenditure is $4,000,000 less than that of his predecessor. Although he will explain that perhaps to the satisfaction of hon. gentlemen on -his own side of the House, he will not explain it to the satisfaction of hon. gentlemen on this side of the House or of the people of the Dominion of Canada, if the expenditure in 1910-1911 under the Liberal Administration was $7,009,822 and in 1914-1915 under the Conservative Administration, $13,561,375.

The hon. gentleman, in
stating the expenditure of the preceding regime, omitted to note the fact that all the drill-halls and public buildings in connection with the militia were charged to public works.
So they are now.

So they are now. I am
including them in the statement I have

made of $2,355,000. You cannot get away from it; it is there in the Public Accounts, it is there in the Estimates. I have given correctly the amount that is being expended for militia in the Dominion of Canada to-day and it represents $2 a head. The minister comes and tells us-it is a pretty story and reads almost like a poem -that he is establishing drill-halls everywhere, and concerning every public expenditure from 1896 down to the present time, whether for the Grand Trunk Pacific or anything else, the minister sees in that expenditure Jwhat was purchased or accomplished but the number of drill-halls that might have been constructed with the money. His mind is obsessed with drill-halls; it is absolutely taken up with soldiers and drill. He can go no further and see no further. He does not seem to realize that what the people want is a fair expenditure for militia, but iwhat they want still more is to have the revenues of this Dominion used for the development of our latent resources and not for the promotion of a warlike spirit. The Minister of Militia wholly mistakes the temper and idea of the people of Canada if he continues on the same line he. has been following since 1911. Why, let us look where these sums for drill-halls have been expended. He has spent in the province of Ontario alone upon drill-ha'ls $1,154,800, and he has put them in the following places:	Kincardine, Mount Forest, Wingham, Watford-small places ranging from two to six thousand people. These drill-halls he put up, he tells us, that the	young	men	might	meet atnight to receive physical instruction, that	they	might receive	education
along the lines of drill; and above all, as we may judge from what we know of this chivalrous Minister of Militia, that they may meet the young ladies and see that a good time is had during the evening. Bui take the whole list, and you will find that with the exception of two places in the province of Ontario, these drill halls for the culture of the youth and beauty-as the minister put it-of the province, had been established where Tory candidates were returned in 1911. As to the rest of the places, why, the young people may grow up stunted, untrained, undrilled, but the minister's answer is: You returned a Grit candidate and are without the pale.

If I may be permitted a question, would the hon. gentleman 
name a riding in Ontario represented by a Grit where a drill ball could be put?

Sarnia. The site has been bought and paid for; it is lying there,-but a Grit was returned and so the minister will not build the drill hall. That is as near home as I know, and the minister can take what comfort out of it he may; it is a shining example of a Grit representative and no armoury.
May I ask another question?
Certainly.

Would he undertake
to draw for this House, or have some one else draw, a plan for the site at Sarnia? It is like a pismire, narrow in the middle and large at either end, fronting on two streets.

It may be, but if you are to take that description of it politically, it remarkably resembles himself.. He asked for an example, and I have given him one. And so you have it all along the line-for the Grits nothing, for the Tories culture and drill halls. I do not know how it is in British Columbia; one would1 naturally suppose there must be a drill hall there on every side line. However that may be, certain it is that it is,absolutely true that the minister stands here to-day and justifies his huge expenditure on drill halls since 1911 by telling us that he wishes the youth of this country to be brought up in a proper way, to receive physical drill, mental drill, and moral drill-
And spiritual drill.

Yes, so he said, and I am indebted to my hon. friend for that word. But the cold fact remains, and he cannot get away from it, that though he preaches this lofty doctrine, he practises it only so far as ridings that have returned Tories are concerned. It is a lovely sight, this man of beautiful ideals whose spirit soars above the clouds when he thinks out these Utopian plans. We cannot but feel that if long ago he had been allowed to come into this mundane sphere and arrange for the culture of the young people-especially during the last fifteen years-he would have so greatly affected the career of the Dominion. Yet he only spends the public money where his henchmen are true to his party.
Mr. GERALD V. WHITE: What about the drill-hall in South Renfrew.
I |Said there were two exceptions. My hon. friend evidently does not know his own county.
I know it better than the hon. gentleman does.

I have had some experience of it, and the hon. gentleman was not in the running. I believe the minister said in the course of his remarks this afternoon that about 73,000 men belonged to the militia of the Dominion of Canada,
Mr. SAM. HUGHES:	There are 77,000
regular militia, not counting cadets.
Mr. PARDEE. I understood the hon. minister to say 73,000. The Minister of Militia has a force of 73,000 men, some of them, I take it, volunteers, few of them on the permanent force and many of them honorary colonels. With a permanent force of about 73,000 men and the remainder volunteers, who are called out annually to drill, and who, I understand, are no expense to the country except during the time of that annual drill, it appears to me, and to many people in the Dominon with Whom I have discussed this matter, to he an extraordinary thing that the headquarters staff and the expenses of its upkeep should assume such tremendous proportions. Expenditures upon the headquarters staff of the militia to March 31, 1913, amounted to $103,309.37 and this year the hon. Minister of Militia is asking for $205,000. To expend upon this staff, most of whom, I take it, live in the city of Ottawa, some in Toronto, some in London, and some in the northern divisions, that large sum for the supervision of 70,000 volunteers and 3,000 regulars; to expend that money in salaries and gold lace is nothing more or less than an unwarranted taxation of the people of Canada. Here are some of the salaries; I shall read only a few of them:
Major General C. C. Mackenzie, Chief of General Staff, $7,500 ; Major General Macdonald, $4,000; Majer General Lessard, $3,000; Colonel Williams, $3,000; Colonel Rutherford, $4,000 ; Colonel Biggar, $3,500.
These amounts, together with expenditures for travelling expenses and upkeep of the general headquarters staff, run up to an enormous total. It would seem to me that that expenditure is wholly unwarranted.
What has the increase been since 1911?

I do not know. Let me say in conclusion that, having regard to
the militia expenditures and to the whole facts	of the matter, it is apparent, as I said in a speech not long ago, that the present Minister of Militia has gone more or less military mad.	He is absolutely obsessed with
militarism; it is his one thought and aim from the time he gets up in the morning until he goes to bed at night. I am wholly in favour of a militia; I believe that the young men of our country should be properly taught, but I am absolutely opposed to a militia which is not commensurate with the needs of the country in every respect.
I do believe that if the minister is well advised he will follow in the footsteps of his predecessor; he will dispel from his mind the idea that we should continually prepare for war with an absolutely unseen foe. If he is well advised he will devote the resources of this country more to the arts of peace than to the arts of war and thereby bring credit to himself and vastly more satisfaction to the people of the Dominion of Canada.
Can the minister now give me the information he promised me this afternoon with regard to the length of time the officers remained in Europe in the years 1907, 1908 and 1909 and 1910?
In some cases they spent two or three months of the year, sometimes longer.
Would the average for the years mentioned be six or eight months?	.

I should imagine that
would be the average.
As I understand it, they were taking a staff course.

Some were taking the
staff course, some minor courses.

Does my hon. friend consider there is any fair comparison between men who seriously go to a college or institution of knowledge to become proficient in their profession, which we must assume was the object of their going in previous years, and the exhibition which the Canadian officers made last year in junketting through Europe with a lot of ladies in automobiles? My hon. friend comes to this House and wants to make the people of this country believe that because they did not spend as much money last year as during a number of previous years, they should be commended. I tell my hon.

friend, following up the line of argument advanced by the hon. member for Lambton, while I do object to the expenditure of this enormous amount of money I object even more strongly to the manner in which it is being expended. When I think of the Minister of Militia of Canada, a man who ought to set an example to the rest of the people of Canada, going through Europe as he went last year, even as shown by the return brought down here-and I imagine we have only a little of the story-every Canadian ought to blush with shame to think of such a thing. He takes twenty or twenty-one officers. He says they are members of the ordinary active militia. They went to Europe. I do not know how long they stayed in England but they went to France and they had the automobiles from the 2nd of September until the middle of October.
How much per day?

I find from the return
that they paid altogether some $7,000 or $8,000 for these automobiles. Just think of it, a lot of Canadian officers going over there and travelling all over Europe with a fleet of automobiles at an expenditure of $7,000 or $8,000! My hon. friend says they saw the manoeuvres and learned so much about the art of war. My hon. friend does not believe that; he knows they did not learn anything about the art of war. He knows it was only a lot of his Tory officers and friends whom he took over there to have a good time, and the people of this country are paying the bill. I am not justifying the amounts of money spent in previous years; I think too much has been expended on the militia in previous years, and I have tried to make that plain every time I have spoken in this House. I do not altogether justify it. I think if $35,000 or $40,000 was spent in sending officers to the other side, the money might have been nearly wasted but they were at least attempting to do something. When my hon. friend went to Europe last year with his friends they were not attempting to do anything except to have a good time. My hon. friend -says it cost $24,000. As I figure from the return it cost nearly $35,000. There is an expenditure of $24,262 given in the return; but in addition to that the officers were paid, according to their rank, practically $4,000, and they had $10 a day each for allowance. That brings it up to $34,000 or $35,000.
Those items are included in the $24,000.

I am glad to know that. The way the question was answered, one would be led to believe that these items were in addition to the $24,000. Now, what earthly military knowledge could my hon. friend and his political friends obtain in scooting from France to Switzerland, from Switzerland to Germany, from Germany to Belgium, and from Belgium back to France with a lot of automobiles and having a glorious good time ? What earthly military knowledge could they gain in a series of excursions like that ?

My hon. friend has twice repeated that these officers were political friends of the Minister of Militia. My hon. friend has forgotten that the minister stated this afternoon that there were more Liberals than Conservatives in the party.
I did not hear the minister make that statement.
He did make that statement.
I think my hon. friend must be in error. .
I am not in error. The minister made the statement this afternoon that there was a majority of Liberals in the company that went to the old country last year!
I shall ask the minister.
Perhaps the minister might explain what military advantage was gained by the expenditure of $24,000.

I never inquired into the politics of the members of the party. I knew that Colonel McLeod was a Tory, and Dave Watson of Quebec. I have been informed that there were one more Liberals than Tories. I am very sorry; I should have had more Tories-but they were good fellows.
I was right, the hon. member did not say that before.
He said it this afternoon. It was on the strength of his statement that I corrected my hon. friend.

My hon. friend also says that he never inquired into their politics. He told about one gentleman from Halifax who had taken an active part against the Premier at the polls. I assume in that case he must have been a Liberal. He brought the officer up here and gave him a lecture and told him to go back home and be good and then took him on this trip. My hon. friend wants the people to believe that these officers have received

some military training, that they have learned something about the art of war. My hon. friend does not believe that. There is not a man sitting behind him who believes that. The officers who went there would not, on their honour, state that they believed it, because they know better. No matter who they may be they know that they simply went over there and had a good time at the country's expense. I was amused not long ago when the Minister of Trade and Commerce, a gentleman whom I think would like to administer the affairs of the country on an economical basis, was discussing subsidies to the steamship lines. There were two little steamship lines running out of Pictou, one I think to Cape Breton and one to Antigonish, the subsidies coming to $3,000 or $4,000 altogether. The minister thought he could save $1,000 of this and amalgamated them. It was pointed out that it was a mistake and caused all sorts of trouble and the minister admitted it, he said the darn thing had given him more trouble than anything he had ever had to deal with. I thought then that he should have handed it over to the Minister of Militia who does not economize on a few thousand dollars, but talks in hundreds of thousands of dollars. He sizes up everything in the way of expenditure by drill-halls and tens of thousands of dollars. The hon. member for Lambton has pointed out that the minister had gone militia mad I think his own friends will admit that; it has become a mania with the hon. gentleman. If we can believe what he tells us this afternoon he is willing to spend half the revenue of Canada on the militia if we will give him the money to expend. He sees the force of our criticism. He has been getting hauled over the coals by his own friends or he would not have made the speech he did to-day, because his whole speech was a justification for his expenditure. He went through some jugglery of figures to try to show that he did not spend as much as the former minister. I could not follow him, probably that is my misfortune. There is no doubt that the minister's statement was plain, but I am satisfied that no member of this House understood him any more than my hon. friend from Lambton and I could. Does the Minister of Militia think that he can convince any reasonable elector in the Dominion of Canada that he has spent $4,000,000 less in the last year than his predecessor did on the militia? That is what he says. He does not believe it, he knows it is not true. He knows that from the public accounts he
will find that in the year 1911, $6,868,000 was expended on the militia and in 1913 they spent $9,114,533, and this year, outside of his drill-halls which are being paid for by the public Works Department, he is asking for $10,867,000; and he hopes that some man in the country will be fool enough to believe him when he makes the statement that in 1911-12 he spent $4,000,000 less than his predecessor. This is only a sample of the kind of argument my hon. friend puts up, and which he is compelled to put up in order to satisfy the grumblings of the people behind him; because, if the truth were known, members on the Government side of the House are just as much disgusted as gentlemen on this side. If this money was being honestly expended for the benefit of the people it would not be so bad. My hon. friend said this afternoon that no money gets back into the pockets of the people so quickly as money spent on the militia. That is true as regards money that goes to the real militia, but my hon. friend took care not to tell us just how much goes to the real militia. Just look at his Estimates. He only wants $2,000,000 for annual drill; that is for the real men; the
74,000	in the active militia, and he is spending nearly $14,000,000 altogether. It is true he is spending $2,300,000 for the permanent force, but so far as the active militia is concerned he is only asking for $2,000,000. In addition to that theTe is something for clothing-an item of $800,600; that would include both the permanent and the active forces. Then there is something for contingencies. The difficulty with my hon. friend is that he has a permanent staff big enough for an army of half a million men. That is the whole trouble. Two hundred and five thousand dollars goes on fuss and feathers, for a lot of men living on the country who are not earning a dollar, and not contributing a dollar to the wealth of the country; men who aTe getting salanes which would be princely in any other walk of life. I want to tell my hon. friend that he had better set the whole lot of these gentlemen to earning their own living. He has to have a certain numbeT of officials, I admit, but to spend $205,000 to keep officers, who do nothing, in gold lace, is absurd. The money would be far better expended in the ordinary walks of peace. Take here at Ottawa: $89,000, according to the statement placed in our hands, is to be spent on the permanent staff in Ottawa alone. When you go down on Slater street you would almost think that we were in the midst of an active campaign. About every other man you

see is going around with brass buttons and gold lace. Do you think, Mr. Chairman, that in a country where we have the ordinary civil officers there is any need of these men going around in uniform? It is no wonder the minister laughs, he is ashamed of it himself?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Can the hon. member tell the House whether this permanent staff is any larger to-day than when the present minister took office?

I do not know how
much larger it is, but I want to tell the Min:ster of Marine and Fisheries that I am not excusing the former minister. I have said that here a good many times. The permanent staff of this country is a disgrace to Canada, and they have so many of these officers that they cannot even do the business of the country. I know what I am talking about. Unfortunately I have a little business to do with the Department of Militia. A company of which I am a director has to render a bill to these gentlemen once a month. It is only a small amount, about $8 or $10, but the moment a dispute arises we always figure on firing the whole thing away because the account would cost more to collect than it is worth. It takes two or three months to get a little $5 account settled, and the reason is this: They have so many of these officers that they have to provide something for them to do. The moment any business comes in it has to go through the whole machinery; it goes through half a dozen officers' hands and through half a dozen different offices. It goes from Woodstock to Fredericton, and from Fredericton to Halifax, and from there to Ottawa, and the Lord knows where after that; and it is weeks and months before you get the thing back. This has to be done in order to justify the existence of these gentlemen. If they were not given something to do there would be trouble. Just let me give an illustration of how they provide work for these officials. This is something that took place at the headquarters staff on Slater street. Not very long ago a gentleman wrote a very polite note to the department asking for a map or plan of some kind. Without giving names, I have here the exact transcript of the thing as it came back:
Letter passed through five stages.
1.	Letter received in department and noted.

2.	Letter endorsed thus:
'D.G.F.S.-For action' and then passed on.
3.	Letter next endorsed thus:
'A.D.M.S.-For action please-G.E.M ' D.G.F.S.
and again passed on.
4.	L- tter next endorsed thus:
'D G.E.S.-Sent to-day-
'M. Anderson, Major Assistant,
Director of Military Surveys.' and once more passed on.
5.	Letter next endorsed thus:
'To note Min. 4.'
'G. S. Maunsell, Lt.-Col. R. E. D.G.E.S.' and then returned with the map.
Have you a key to the abbreviations?
No.
Does the hon. gentleman say what the correspondent was asking for?
A map.
It is the rule to refuse to give military plans to any person.

My hon. friend can talk after a little while. This gentleman was not asking for any secrets; he was not a traitor or a rebel; he was not trying to get into the secrets of the department; he was a loyal member of Parliament, who i's sitting not more than a hundred feet away from where I stand.
Was he a Nationalist?
No.

I happen to be an officer of the militia and a commanding officer. If any maps are issued to me, for any reason, I have to return them to the department immediately they are done with. I think that is a very good thing. Topographical ' maps of this country, plans of fortresses-

I object to my hon. friend making a speech. He need not get excited; he will have a chance later on. I did not say that this man was asking for a topographical map or for a plan of a fortress; it was only a little bit of a blue print, something which he had a perfect right to get, and the fact that he got it is the best evidence that it was all right. The minister's officers would not have given it to him if it had not been all right.
The fortress was taken.

No, i-t was protected. The man got the map all right, but, instead

of getting it by the next mail, as in the case of any ordinary bnsiness concern, he had to wait till the letter had travelled around this circuitous route. It had to pass through all these officers' hands to justify their existence. If these letters were answered like the Minister of Railways, or the Minister of the Interior, or any other minister of this Government would answer them, four out of every five of these gold-laced chaps down there would have to be dismissed. These gentlemen are kept down there for the glorification of the minister. If the minister had only two or three officials down on Slater street, there would be no officer there to salute him when he went down there in the morning, and it would not be necessary for members of Parliament to get a pass in order to go down there to do business. It would be an ordinary business transaction
Has my hon. friend-
Now, what is the trouble again?

I would like the hon.
gentleman to be fair. I would like to ask him if there has been any addition to the number of officers on the headquarters' staff since the present minister took charge of the department?
I answered that question.

Another question:	Who
initiated the pass system that the hon. gentleman speaks so much about?

I answered that question once before. I say that there has been an Increase in the number of officers-I cannot tell how many-but there was an increase of eight or nine according to the statement, I think, last year. I am admitting that the former minister was guilty, not as guilty as the present minister, because it would be almost an impossibility to find a man in Canada who was quite as crazy on military matters as the present minister. I know that the hon. member for North Simcoe is looking for his shoes and if the conditions were changed and the hion. member for North Simcoe was in the present minister's place I do not think he would be hardly as bad as the present minister. I presume that is the reason why he has not been taken in; he does not fit in with the conditions. It would be a pretty serious
matter to get rid of a lot of these gold lace gentlemen.

Now, just a minute; I
would like to enlighten the hon. gentleman on that point. When the other Government was in office I was a member of this House, an officer of the militia-
Now, Mr. Chairman. Some hon. MEMBERS. Order, order.

I can-
Some bon. MEMBERS:	Order, order.

Oh, I am not-
