My horn, friend (Mr. Currie) asked me a question and I answered him as best I knew how. If my hon, friend wants to ask another question I am willing to give him an opportunity but I do not intend to allow my horn, friend to make a speech until I am through.

I presume the hon. gentleman desires to be fair?
10 p.m. Mr. CARVELL: Certainly.

That is a fair question
and if my hon. friend was compelled to sit an hour and a half I do not think he was properly treated.
Has the present minister ever done that to you?

He has not done that
with me because I have only been down

there but once since he was minister and when I was there I found a whole regiment of officials around. I found the department bristling with brass buttons. Officials were standing every five or six feet apart from the time I went into the building until I got out of it.
Did they salute?

No, amd they did not
ask jine for a pass; they let me go in. If my hon. friend has been held up by officials during the present Administration I am sorry for him. But I seem to have disturbed my hon. friend. Possibly I have called up unpleasant thoughts to him; I am sorry for having done so. I did not intend to say anything personal. He is youing in the world yet. It is true that he is a full fledged colonel, he is getting along very well and he probably may get to be Minister of Militia some day. He has yet twenty-five years ahead of him, he will have obtained a little more information and I believe that if he does reach this high position he will not be as bad as the present Minister of Militia because I think that is almost impossible.
I have tried to point out to the minister the way they are running things on this headquarters' staff. Let us go down to the provinces. Go down, for instance, to the little province of New Brunswick. You will find a lot of this outfit around Fredericton. I do not know how many there are there. You will see them on the streets, they have great big barracks, and when you go to Halifax you find them more numerous and the barracks much bigger. They have all these expensive men just simply to sign things like this:	' for
action-place-D.G.M.,' and so on. That is all they are doing. One good clerk at a salary of $1,000 a year in New Brunswick- and he would not be employed all his time -and two men at Halifax could do the whole business. No matter how little the thing may be that you want done, you have to have a man sent down all the way to Halifax to do it. This applies to the most trifling little thing you could imagine. Not long ago I spoke to the minister about a piece of property in my own town. There was no question about it, they had the deed of the property, and the thing was perfectly plain. I wanted him to give me some information about it, and he said: I will have to send my engineer officer down there. The result was that the engineer officer was sent all Carveiy
the way from Ottawa to Woodstock with nothing in the world for him to do that I could see, because they had had three or four sets of officers doing the same thing, and I suppose it cost $100 to get this gentleman down there. That is going on all over the country. These are things that the people are getting tired of. If they had been spending this money on the militia, if the men and the boys, as the minister calls them, who go out and drill, were the ones to get some of this money the people would not have so much fault to find, but when you have one string of officers after another string of officers travelling around the country and squandering money the people most decidedly object. Not only do you pay the headquarters' staff $205,000, but you pay something like $100,000 for travel and transportation.
$200,000 for transport.

No, that is the transport of the militia generally, but there is something for the transport of this headquarters' staff as well. I see here that there is a charge of $30,000 for the travelling expenses of the headquarters' and district staffs. Add that to $205,000, and you have $235,000, in addition to which there are some thousands of dollars of contingencies. I suppose you will have close upon $300,000 as the amount which is being used up by a lot of these men, not one of whom earns really a thousand dollars a year. I know that I am not making myself popular with these gentlemen in talking in this way, but I am telling the minister the truth. I am trying to tell him how the people look upon it, and if he thinks he is going to make himself and the Government popular, and that they will be pleased by such figures as were recited here this afternoon, he is very much mistaken.
I congratulate the minister on the fact that he has sobered down a little this evening, and that he has given this matter a little more serious thought than I have ever seen him give it before.
The minister stated this afternoon that one of the objects of this organization was to teach men how to shoot. I agree that that is a laudable object. If he is going to have a militia force that is to be of any earthly use he must have one composed of men who are able to handle a rifle or a big gun or a piece of artillery. But it is simply pitiable when you consider the amount of money that is being expended on the really necessary portion of the militia. If you

take the rifle associations of the Dominion of Canada, organizations which really try to do something to carry out the excuse for the existence of the militia, you will find in the summary under grants to associations and bands, the magnificient sum of $80,900. That includes all the little associations throughout the country. I presume that sum would include eight armouries or drill-halls?
Yes.
The hon. minister has allowed eight drill-halls per year for rifle shooting and things of that kind.
A drill-hall is a unit.

Yes, a drill-hall is a unit of value. In my own province of New Brunswick, which is not large, there is an association to which I belonged and which had seventy or eighty members-I think I have seen over 100 members there. The Provincial Rifle Association of New Brunswick is getting the magnificient sum of $1,300 out of the $14,000,000 that the minister is spending on gold lace, frills, fuss and feathers.
There is ammunition in addition to that.
Yes, 200 rounds of ammunition.
If my hon. friend belonged to an association-
I have belonged to an association as long as my hon. friend has, and I know as much about it as he does.
Do you hope to be a colonel?

No, I have not any
hopes, because I know that my hon. friend will never make me a colonel as a reward of merit; it will be only as a punishment. I find that the Provincial Rifle Association of Nova Scotia gets the magnificient sum of $1,600, and the whole Dominion of Canada recevies for bands and rifle associations only $80,900. The very thing that means something to the militia, the very thing for which the militia exists, is absolutely thrown to the winds and the money is squandered in the manner described by my hon. friend from West Lambton (Mr. Pardee) and by myself. If my hon. friend did not want his own glorification, but a real militia force, he would spend $800,000 instead of $80,000 for this purpose. It must 217
be remembered that all the rifle associations are included in this; and if my hon. friend from North Simcoe (Mr. Currie) will look at the details, he will find that the Militia Department gives a rifle association thirty ot forty dollars and expects it to exist on that. A staff colonel will spend twice that amount of money in making a trip that is not necessary.
My hon; friend has certain branches of the service which may just as well for all practical purposes be eliminated entirely. I am speaking now about the artillery and the engineers, and I have some practical knowledge in regard to these branches of the militia. Not only is the present artillery of Canada of no use, but it would be a menace in time of trouble because the officers are not properly trained. My hon. friend knows that modern artillery has no value whatever excepting in the hands of highly technically trained officers. He has battery after battery of field artillery and has not a qualified officer, let alone a technically trained one. My hon. friend is not doing anything to remedy this condition of affairs. When he speaks about sending instructors throughout the country, he knows that he has sent a few, but they are not doing anything. My hon. friend will tell us that his predecessor is liable for this condition of affairs but he is spending $4,000,000 on the artillery-
There are other armaments and equipment connected with that.

Then my statement was practically correct. If my hon. friend is going to add thirty or forty new batteries and make them of any service, he will have to spend three or four thousand dollars in educating officers. He is not doing it; he is not trying to do it. My hon. friend does not seem to appreciate the value of this at all. His sole idea is to have something for his own glorification, something for show and exhibition, but nothing in the world for real value. It would be a crime to send the artillery of this country into active service under present conditions. I am sorry to make this statement, because I was an officer of a battery of artillery, but I am telling the minister the honest truth. When I come to the engineers corps, I think they are in an even worse plight than is the artillery. These are technical branches of the service, and yet practically nothing is being done in order to make them any better than they were ten years ago. If the minister will take some ol these mil-



lion dollars and spimd the money intelligently, it will not be so bad, ibut the money i3 simply being squandered. Nevertheless the minister makes a speech of two hours and a half-
Two hours exactly.

And he thinks the
whole thing a huge joke. He gets annoyed when a member asks him a question, becomes almost ungentlemanly in one instance when I asked him what I thought to be a reasonable and fair question. He apparently feels that all he has to do is to travel throughout the country in special trains; to spend $20,000 in going to the old country; to ask every man to take off his hat and hurrah for Colonel Hughes; to take the English officers who come out here, I think for no very good purpose, to Conservative picnics to have their photographs taken-I have a photograph here which I shall send to the minister if he wishes it.

With the Borden
Club?
Yes, the whole thing- the Prime Minister, General Hamilton and a lot more of these chaps at a Conservative picnic. The minister does not appreciate what it means to be a Minister of Militia.

Were they against
Home Rule at that picnic?
I do not know.
It is a very appropriate aggregation.

Yes, especially for a
minister who pretends to be a non-political Minister of Militia. The minister has three or four things to explain that he forgot to explain in his two hours' speech this afternoon. He tells us: Oh, I am spending this money to elevate the moral tone of the young men and women of this country; I am building drill-halls in order that the young men and women may meet there on Saturday afternoons and improve their manners and morals and even their religion. Well, Sir, the militia is a different kind of organization from what it was when I belonged to it if it helps anybody's morals, manners or religion. I have no son, but if I had, I should want to keep pretty close to him while he belonged to the militia of Canada, judging from past experience. It

is true, the hobby of the minister just now is temperance. We have had that pretty well aired here this afternoon. He is going round preaching to the Women's Christian Temperance Union organization and telling them what a great temperance organizer he is and what good things he has done-no more liquor in the camps and all that kind of thing. He was at nearly all the camps last year, and he knows-or ought to know- that there was not a camp in Canada in which liquor did not flow like water-not an officers' mess in which there was not liquor galore. Take the case of Sussex, or take the case of Petawawa, I know officers who were at those camps, and I speak of them because I know something about them. If the minister says there was no liquor in those messes, then he is a greater innocent than I give him credit for being. Oh, no, he knows better. When he makes these statements, he is simply sailing under false colours. Why, we had an illustration here given by my hon. friend from Sherbrooke. The minister takes their building off the hands of a political club and pays the rent. They are running the club and selling the liquor-and as a club that is all Tight; I . have no fault to find with it, for I know that there is probably not a club in Canada that has not the right to sell liquor. But the minister is paying the rent of this club, and the country, to that extent, is standing its expense, and they aTe selling the liquor. And then the minister will go to the Women's Christian Temperance Union organization and say: Look at me, the only real temperance Minister of Militia. I hope the minister will practise what he preaches. The greatest objection I have to the militia of Canada is that it is not a temperance organization but a 'boozorium.'
Mr. SAM. HUGHES: That is unparliamentary.
Why, I have heard the minister himself use it.
But I had to retract it.

But I am sure the minister does not want me to retract it, because he knows it is true. Now if he were honestly trying to keep liquor out of these camps he would be doing a wonderful thing. But he is not doing it. He holds out these drill halls as of great advantage to the country. I have one in my own town. It cost $30,000 or $32,000. It is big enough for the purpose for which it was designed- perhaps a little too big, but big enough. The minister ought to know, and I think

he does know, that instead of that being used for the moral and religious uplift of the people, it is not used for anything. Nobody is allowed to go there except members of the militia. They have their club, and the report is that it is not a strictly temperance organization. However, that is their affair. Not long ago they had a fight of nearly a year's duration before even the regimental band could get the right to use a room there. The hon. minister talks about people generally getting the use of these drill halls on Saturday afternoon and so on. Why, the drill hall is locked up. And if a Liberal were to show his nose there, I really believe he would be dynamited. The sign is practically up:	Liberals keep out; this is our drill hall. The minister tells us there is no politics in this thing. In my town it is presided over by a strong Conservative-and I am not finding any fault with him. But all over the country these are run as part of the Tory machine. What is the use of the minister talking; the militia never was so much a political machine as it has come to be since the present minister began to preside over it. There is not a member within the sound of my voice on whatever side of the House he may sit, but knows that what I am saying is true-the militia is just one great Tory machine from Halifax to Vancouver. The only Liberals allowed are those of whom they are trying to make proselytes. Yet the minister travels around and declares that there is no politics in this thing.
Now, I have pointed out to the minister a few of the things to which I take very serious objection ill the militia. And I know I am voicing the sentiments of many of those who sit behind him as well as of those on this side. The members who sit behind him are not in a position to tell him publicly what they think about it, but, fortunately, those on this side utc not in that position. I say, Sir, that it is almost a disgrace that $14,000,000 a year of the public revenues of this country should be spent in militia matters. Who in the world are we going to fight with? Let us talk that over as a matter of business for one moment. Against whom are we arming? Why is it necessary to have three or four millions spent on artillery and to have 140,000 araied and trained men, which is the number the minister says he wants, to have? He said he had something like 77,000 now, and he has another 70,000 ready, but has not the arms and equipment for them. It is a blessing for Canada that 217i
he has not the arms and equipment for these men. And, let me tell him he has not got 77,000 men in Canada ready to do service-he has not got 50,000. Many of the figures he has given have no better basis than his own vivid imagination. He himself has admitted that 25 per cent of his enlistment did not go to camp last year.
. He said this afternoon that they were 'relieved.' He knows very well that he could not get them to go to camp.
I do not know that.

Then, he ought to know. He will hardly find a rural corps in eastern Canada up to its strength, the reason being that they cannot get the men to enlist. And there is not a rural corps in Canada that does not take into camp men from forty-five to sixty-five yeaTs of age. They shave off their beards and give assumed names when the paymaster comes around. The minister knows that; he is not so innocent as not to know it. But even with all these tricks they cannot get up to their strength. It is true that the cavalry and artillery are nearly up to their strength. If. a man has a horse, that horse brings pay and brings the man too. I can tell him that there are some corps where not a horse can get in unless it brings in a man also. And so they staTt recruiting horses and not men. The minister knows all these things, and yet he stands here and paints a glowing picture of the enthusiasm existing all over Canada for the militia service. He knows that they have to take into camp old men, as I have said. He knows that especially regarding the engineer corps-and I think that is the most useless of all. He knows that every year they have twenty-five or thirty-five horses a year that simply stand on the picket lines and do nothing but haul water and draw their $1.25 a day and forage. They would not be able to get one-half their enlistment if they did not take those horses along. My hon. friend painted a picture this afternoon which would seem to indicate that the people of the country are dying to go to war. My advice to the minister is to quit this nonsense. Instead of trying to raise a force of 140,000 or 150,000 men, let him cut it down to 35,000 or 40,000; let him give them officers who are of some value, especially in the technical branches of the service. Give the men regular and frequent target practice; give them not 200 but 1,000 rounds of ammunition. Give the artillery technical

officers and ample target practice. I admit that this would be expensive, but the artillery are of no use unless they are efficient. My hon. friend talks about having all these men ready to go out at a moment's notice in case of war. After all, what does twelve days in camp really mean? The man who goes to camp for twelve days has no more knowledge of the rudiments of war than he had twelve days before he went to camp. I have endeavoured to point out the sins of the omission and commission of my hon. friend the minister and I have endeavoured to portray the facts as they really exist. If I can bring my hon. friend down to earth and get him to view this matter along reasonable and rational lines, my words shall not have been in vain.

I wish to draw the attention of the minister to the fact that in the printed information he has sent out he says:
Compared with 1913-14, there is a decrease of $71,905.
Are there to be any further amounts in the Supplementary Estimates?
I hope so.
Is this statement which I have read, then, not a misrepresentation?
Not at all; these are the Main Estimates.

A few days ago I put a question to the hon. minister respecting the Royal Canadian band taking part in a certain demonstration in the city of Halifax. The questions and the answers were as follows:
1.	Who authorized the hand of the Royal Canadian Regiment to take part in a demonstration in connection with a public meeting in the Province building, Halifax, on the evening *of Wednesday, April 8, 1914?,
2.	Who requested the services of the said band to take part in the demonstration?
3.	Was any payment made for the services *of said band, and by whom was payment made?
4.	If payment has not been made, is there any charge made against any person in connection with such service?
Mr. Sam. Hughes:
1.	The officer commanding the Royal Canadian Regiment, under the provisions of para-raph 875, K. R. & O. (Canada), 1910, as amended by H.Q. 35-1-5, of 7th March, 1914.
2.	P. Pennington Bligh, Esq.
3.	No.
4.	A charge of $45 has been made against C. R. Hoben, Esq.
Is the hon. minister in a position to say whether or not that charge has been paid?

I have no information on the subject; it will be paid.

Mr.' KYTE: I endeavoured also to call the attention of the hon. minister a few days ago to another incident in connection with the Royal Canadian Regiment band at Halifax, which only goes to show how true is the assertion of the hon. member for Carleton that the militia force of the province of Nova Scotia is becoming an adjunct of the Tory party. It is well known to people who read the newspapers in the province of Nova Scotia that a very serious libel was published upon the Legislature of that province by a newspaper in the city of Halifax. A special committee of the Legislature was appointed for the purpose of inquiring into this libel. One of the witnesses, having refused to answer a proper and legitimate question which was put to him, was ordered to be committed to the common jail of the city of Halifax for forty-eight hours. The moment he was committed to jail, the Royal Canadian band, acting under the instructions, I have no doubt, of the Tory mayor of the city of Halifax, came out in full regimentals for the purpose of serenading this man who was incarcerated for gross libel upon the Legislature of the province of Nova Scotia. My informant says:
Royal Canadian band in King's uniform, with soliders in uniform at their head, carrying Union Jack, paraded Saturday to serenade McCurdy imprisoned in county jail by warrant of Speaker for misbehaviour in refusing to answer questions asked by Committee of House of Assembly.
I endeavoured to ascertain from the minister the other day what authority was given to permit the band to commit this second offence upon the common decency of the people of the city of Halifax, but I was ruled out of order. As we have plenty of time to discuss the question now, I would like to ask the hon. Minister of Militia and Defence under what authority the band came out under the circumstances which I have related.

Information relating to this band was laid before the House in answer to a question asked by the hon. member himself, I think, yesterday or the day before. I received complaint about this terrible band a short time ago to the effect that they had actually turned out with the Hibernian Society, carrying a Union Jack with a bit of green ribbon tied around the flag pole over the flag. I now have another complaint that the band turned out to serenade some poor fellow who had been locked up in jail; about that I know nothing. There is no reason in the world why the band should not turn out if it is paid,

so long as the officer in command of the district, who is responsible for the band, inquires into the nature of the proceedings in which the band is to take part and gives it his authority to turn out. If my hon. friend holds a meeting in Halifax, I shall be delighted, provided he pays for their services, if the band turns out and plays for him or for any other decent person who comes along and engages them. I was delighted that they played for the Hibernians; I would be delighted if they would play on the 12th of July for the Orangemen, and if they place a bit of orange ribbon upon the flag pole I shall not raise any more objection to it than I did to the tying of a green ribbon to the flag pole on St. Patrick's day.

The hon. Minister of Militia might well have enumerated other occasions on which objections were raised to regimental bands coming out on occasions if not of a public, of a quasi-public character. I remember an objection raised by the hon. Minister of Militia himself because soldiers marched on the occasion of a religious celebration held in the city of Montreal. When the hon. Minister of Militia enumerates the numerous objections that are made with regard to bands and regiments of soldiers participating in. events which are not entirely of a public character, he should not forget that he several times raised objections in this House because certain regimental bands and troops in the city of Montreal were allowed to march under the circumstances which I have indicated.

I would like to correct the hon. member right there. I never objected to a band, but I do object, and shall object, to any regiment turning out with arms for any religious procession, I care not what it may be. That is against the law. They must not carry their rifles, that would be contrary to the rule the world over.

I beg to inform the minister that not only did the band serenade McCurdy in jail the other night, but soldiers in uniform marched at the head of the band carrying the Union Jack, and assisted in the serenade of McCurdy in the jail; so evidently the instructions of the minister were not observed.
The man carrying the flag is part of the band and he must wear the uniform.

I have no doubt there has been more flag flying and band playing
since the minister took over the department than ever before. I repeat that the conduct of the band and those in command at Halifax is absolute proof that the militia in Halifax, as well as elsewhere, has become an adjunct of the Tory party.

The only official I have known to do any political work in Halifax was the officer whose case I cited to-day, who stood at the polls and tried to prevent officers and non-commissioned officers and men from voting for the right hon. gentleman who has the honour of being Prime Minister of Canada.

I venture to say that notwithstanding the apparent fair mindedness with which the Minister of Militia and Defence is discussing this question, if the junior member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) or I or any other member supporting the Liberal party required the services of the band in Halifax we could not have it.
Yes, you could.

Or the price would be such as would make the use of the band absolutely impossible. No time would be given for payment, as apparently time has been given to the mayor of Halifax on an account that has not yet been paid, so far as the minister knows. Here is the language of the Minister of Militia and Defence in this House on the 25th November, 1910:
I am opposed to any man wearing the uniform of the militia of this country turning out in honour of any representative of any organization that is not directly under the control or auspices of the State, whether it be clerical or anything else.
The hon. minister has changed his mind on that, as he has on other questions which are germane to what we are now discussing.
I notice that the Minister of Militia visited Toronto the other night and gave an address to certain officers. I have here a press despatch which I assume contains a fairly correct report of his utterance. If it is not correct, of course he will put the committee in possession of the exact language he used:
Toronto, May 2-At the annual dinner of the 48 th Highlanders Sergeants' Mess, last night, the guest of honour was Colonel Sam. Hughes, Minister of Militia, who in replying to the toast of the Canadian Militia, spoke of the relatively high state of efficiency of which the militia of the country has attained, and declared his intention of continuing the policy so long as he remains Minister of Militia, of increasing that efficiency, so that Canada will always he in a position to guard against any danger of attack.
In the course of his remarks Colonel Hughes declared that at the present time he is perpared

to place in the field, tomorrow, if necessary, a force of ffO.OOO men, capable of meeting any enemy, while" throughout Canada, he states, there are 750,000 men ready to take the field at once, and this number he hopes will be doubled by next year.
The politicians who do not see eye to eye with Colonel Hughes on military matters came in for some condemnation when he remarked that he rather liked to have 'these yelping politicians' attack him and that their attack reminded himi of a certain pup near Lindsay, Ont., who regularly used to meet the incoming train and bark at it. To stop to argue with these same politicians Colonel Hughes considered would be on a line with the action of the engineer of the said train if he were to stop it to shy coals at the dog.
Hear, hear.

I did not know that j;he
suggestion of dogs would have raised so
many yelpers. The minister has not denied the language attributed to him and therefore-
I have not been asked to deny it.
I did .ask him whether or not the language attributed to him is -correct.
There is an error. I said that the engineer would be very foolish to stop the train.

Just for the same reason*
the people of this country would be very foolish to continue the services of the hon. minister, and they will not do so any longer than they can help. According to the admission of the Minister of Militia, every politician ini this country, every paid representative of the people who raises his voice in favour of economy in the expenditure of the Department of Militia, is referred to as a yelping politician. That is the term that the Minister of Militia applies to them. I hope that this paragraph will sink down into the minds of the tax payers of this country. We have -a condition existing in Canada such as has not existed for the last seventeen or eighteen years. All over Canada there is unemployment, there is a time of distress. People are organizing charity societies to raise funds to meet the conditions of the working mem in many centres of population. Everybody -admits that it is a time when economy ought to be practised. The Minister of Finance, a few days ago, in delivering his Budget to this House, pointed out the necessity for putting on the brakes and said that he intended, as Minister of Finance, to take into account the

circumstance that this is not an opportune time to engage in any large- expenditure. Every other service of the country is to be
curtailed. I believe that every other minister in the Government except the Minister of Militia is disposed to take the same view of the financial situation as is taken by the Minister of Finance. But if the tax-payers of Canada suggest that the expenditure on militia is the most useless indulged in by -any department of the Government, if the representatives of the people in Parliament should suggest to the minister that he ought to put the brakes upon his -expenditures, the only answer is that they are yelping politicians and he compares them with -his own pup in his own town of Lindsay. The Minister of Militia does not always take himself as seriously as he appears to take himself with regard to this particular matter. Last night, when we were discussing another subject pertaining to his department with reference to the payment of Fenian Raid bounties in Nova Scotia, my hon. friend from Carleton pointed out that a very large sum of money was being paid in Nova Scotia to men who had notactually gone to the front to fight the battles That threatened at that time, whereas, on the other hand, those who actually did go to the front were not receiving the bounty. The Minister of Militia and Defence, in- the face of the fact well known to everybody from Nova Scotia, actually stated that no man in Nova Scotia was paid a dollar for Fenian Raid bounties unless he had gone to the front. I think it is time the people of this -country realized that statements made by the Minister of Militia with respect to expenditures in his department should be taken, not with the usual grain of salt, but with a very considerable modicum of that article.
The hon. minister is determined, it appears, to expend ten per Cent of the total revenue of this country in fuss and feathers, as my hon. friend from Carieton describes it. I remember that two years ago there was summoned from the four corners of this Dominion soldiers of more or less importance, in the military organization. The city of Ottawa had the appearance of a beleaguered -camp for a whole week. One scarcely dared pass through the corridors of this House for fear of tumbling over burnished spurs or having a bayonet run through some vital part of his anatomy. That junketing expedition, brought about

for the glorification of the minister, cost the people of Canada a tidy sum. I did hear very loud complaints not only on the part of hon. gentlemen on this side of the House but from gentlemen on the Government benches as regards this absolutely useless expenditure. I was present at one of the meetings, and I saw- the magnificent manner in which the whole thing was staged. The Minister of Militia in his very best suit of regimentals sat on a sort of raised throne. He had an orderly on one side and an orderly on the other, and whenever he rose to speak the orderlies doffed their hats and bowed low as though they were paying obeisance to a most revered, and exalted deity. All this was for the glorification of the minister, who refers to the representatives of the taxpayers of this country as yelping politicians, and compares them to his pet pup in the town of Lindsay.

I desire to point out that the hon. gentleman never saw any such scene, except in his own disordered imagination. I never sat in uniform at one of the meetings, and the description is a fabrication from start to finish.
Mr. KYTE. The hon. minister would not be the minister if he was not in uniform. I have seen him coming into this House dressed in uniform. If he did not wear feathers he wore a coat of such brilliant colours as to almost dazzle the eyes of hon. members of this House.
I dare say it is contrary to the wishes and spirit of the hon. gentleman to see that scarlet uniform.

The hon. minister presides over the department that has control of the men who have sworn to His Majesty to defend this country and His Majesty on -all occasions, and yet one of the officers of the militia, who occupies a seat in this House, sitting behind the minister, offered his services a few weeks ago to Sir Edward Carson for the purpose of aiding an armed rebellion against law and order in the province of Ulster. The minister is very loyal when interests of a certain element in this country are concerned, but the minister would permit every officer of the militia to bear arms against law and authority if it is on behalf of the Orangemen of Ulster.

Might I correct the hon. gentleman. That just shows his tyrannical spirit. The militia of Canada
are free men when they are not on duty, and the Minister of Militia has no more right to oppose their will than in the case of any other citizen of this country. When not under orders, the men of the militia are as free as any other men.

They are not free
to take arms against the Grown.

That ie not my concern. I want to point out to my hon. friend, and other gentlemen of the committee, that he mistakes the function of an officer in charge of a department if he thinks the minister should undertake to use forcible measures against those who have the right to breathe the free air of Heaven.
Would the minister explain what he means by using forcible measures against those who have the right to breathe the free air of Heaven?
If the hon. gentleman's intelligence cannot interpret it, I am not going to take up the time of the House in doing it for him.

I rise to a point of order and it is this: the hon. member for Richmond (Mr. Kyte) has charged a member of this House with desiring to go and take up arms against His Majesty. That is a very serious charge.
Did he not do it?
If the hon. member says he did not send the telegram, I accept his word.
I 'am not the gentleman at all. The hon. member has made a very serious charge against a member of this House.

If the hon. member that I refer to rises from his seat in this House, and says that he never sent that telegram offering his services to Sir Edward Carson, assuring him that he would fight with him to the last ditch, I am bound to accept his statement; and I will do it with the utmost pleasure, because it will be an assurance to me that there is one more loyal man in Canada than I thought there was.
I think the hon. member had better bring the matter up when the gentleman he refers to is here.
I want to assure my hon. friend that he cannot inspire any member of this House with fear.
If such a charge had been made against a member on that side of the House, I would have been the first to get np and refute it.
If it is true that the telegram was not sent, I shall be very glad to hear it from the lips of the hon. gentleman himself, but I refuse to accept it by proxy.
I rise to a point of order. I do not think it is fair for an hon. member of this House to make such a serious charge against another member during his absence.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I did not understand the hon. member for Richmond to make a charge against any member of this House. The facts recited by the hon. member had reference to a telegram, and that is all.

As I said, if the hon. member will deny sending that telegram, I will be the first to accept his denial. The minister stated a moment ago, as justification of the action of that officer, that the men in the militia were free men, and that they could go and come where they pleased; but under certain conditions they are not free. They are not free in Montreal. I remember that a few years ago the question of their attending a certain quasipublic function in Montreal was the subject of criticism on the part of the present Minister of Militia with respect to his predecessor in that office.
I may point out that when an officer is in uniform he is on duty.

That is the whole point. The hon. minister is willing that they should be on duty under certain circumstances, and under other circumstances he is not willing that they should be on duty. When the hon. member for North Simcoe interrupted me, I was making a statement with respect to the extraordinary amount of money that is being spent from year to year on the militia. The hon. member for Oarleton (Mr. Oarvell) gave some figures with regard to the expenditure of public money in respect to the period when the Liberal Government was in power. But then, we had a sane Minister of Militia who recognized that he had some other duties to perform, that he owed something more to the taxpayers of Canada, than to go around parading with officers in automobiles, touring through Europe and indulging in junketing expeditions from one end of the country to the other from which no value can accrue to the people of the Dominion. The item of the expenditure for militia is one that cannot be too long debated in this House particularly in view of the defiant attitude assumed by the minister in Toronto the other night when he referred to the representatives of the people in this country who endeavoured to reduce the expenditure for militia purpose as yelping politicians.

Mr. NEELY. Perhaps the minister will explain what he did mean. If the minister thinks he is going to get away with that sort of thing he is sadly mistaken, because there are members on this side of the House who are not afraid to take the gloves off with the minister in the House or out of it any time he wishes to discuss public questions or his own department. The minister undertook to tell the House this afternoon that the expenditures of his department were actually decreasing as compared with the expenditures of his predecessor. That, as a statement of fact, is something that must be regarded as being beyond a joke, because it is not very far to the library, and all we have to do is to take the militia Estimates for years past, and in no possible way, by the juggling of figures, can you reach the conclusion reached by the Minister of Militia. Then, if you look at the Auditor General's Report as to what the minister actually does
expend, you are confronted with 11 p.m. this difficulty, that you have to look here and there all through that report, and almost all through Public Works as well as Militia and Sundry Expenditures, to find what the minister is actually expending for the maintenance of the militia, the construction of drill-halls and other appurtenances _ of the militia throughout Canada. The minister, both in this House and out of it, has taken the ground, as stated by my hon. friend for West Lambton (Mr. Pardee) that the people of this country want more money spent on the militia than has been spent in years gone by. I am here to-night to tell him that the people in certain parts of the country, at any rate, whatever they may do in others, and I represent one of those parts, do not want to see the militia expenditure jumping up by leaps and bounds as it is under the administration of the present incumbent of the_ office.
I represent in this House a constituency 108 miles long by 108 miles wide-I would be very glad if it were smaller whether I represented it or not-and I suppose there are some twenty to forty villages and towns in that constituency, varying from 500 population to 2,500 population. I have not heard of any four corners, leaving out the towns and villages in the constituency of Humboldt, having a drill-hall costing the country from ten to fifteen thousand dollars planted there simply because that particular corner happened to cast a good Tory vote in the last election. I have heard of things of that sort in eastern Canada, for instance in the province of Ontario, if I have been correctly informed. In regard to this expenditure on drill-halls in small places throughout Canada and especially is the practice reprehensible in country districts where there is no sign of a militia at all and where these halls are built for the social entertainments of that particular community-I desire to point out that every one of these drill-halls is adding to the fixed cost of the Government of this country. There is the money that is invested not bringing one dollar of revenue to this country; there are the men employed to take care of these buildings, and there is the cost of upkeep and maintenance, year after year. If the hon. minister is allowed to go on with a free hand and build ten, fifteen and twenty thousand dollar drill-halls in little villages and small towns and even at country post offices where there are

neither villages nor towns nor railroads, in a few years the revenue of this country will have to be doubled and trebled to keep up the fixed charges to be paid for these drill-halls that are absolutely useless so far as any permanent benefit to the militia of this country is concerned.
Representing a people who are trying to make Canada a nation by developing her natural resources, by increasing her national wealth, by contributing as they do largely to the Government of this country, I cannot afford to sit still and hear the sentiment uttered by the Minister of Militia in this House and out it that Canada is in favour of increasing her militia expenditures. I do not believe that to be the case. I think the Minister of Militia has been feeling simply his own pulse in this instance and not the pulse of the people when he has made this diagnosis so far as the sentiment of the people in military matters are concerned.
I have not very much criticism to offer of some of the lines of expenditure pursued by the present Minister of Militia since he has taken office. I presume that the question of a little outing with a number of friends across the Atlantic and that sort of thing seems like a pretty good proposition to the minister. After fifteen years in opposition, I presume he came to the conclusion, when he got hold of his present position, that it was about time that he was enjoying himself at the expense of his country having represented it in this Parliament for so many years. These expenses might perhaps be regarded by the minister as incidental, but they go to make up the grand total. I would like to be in a position where I would not have to charge the minister with 
using his position and the department over which he presides in a partisan manner; I would like to think there was * one bright and shining light sitting on the Government benches; but I do not see how anybody in this House can come to the conclusion that the Minister of Militia and Defence is that particular bright and shining light. ister took charge of the affairs of the Department of Militia.

The expenditure of
$199,000 in Port Arthur, and I have no doubt that that will not be the only expenditure, it seems to me to be excessive.
